speechtext: No, I have been here constantly since returning from a trip abroad. If the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) will go back over the last twenty-seven years that I have been in this house he will find that very few members have attended the sessions of parliament more closely than I have done. I believe the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), who is the only older member in the house than I, will at least accord me that. True, I was away in the early part of the session when I was absent from the country; but what I am saying has reference to this particular occasion and the discussion of this bill. I am not speaking of the discussion of ordinary estimates or of any pro forma matter; but here is a bill, the most important measure before the house this session, and there is comparatively little attention being paid to it.

subsubtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Particularly on the opposition side, as the hon. gentleman will agree. Just look!

subsubtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: In all parts of the house.

subsubtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Look opposite; it is pitiable.

subsubtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
In all parts of the house. If the statement gives offence to the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Agriculture I want to assure them that it is not said in any offensive spirit. I mention it merely because I am interested in this measure.
Coming back to the question of housing, I make the suggestion which I have submitted because in my opinion it is one of the things that will go a long way in the direction of reducing the number of unemployed in Canada and it will give the greatest impetus to the development of business; because anyone who has studied the question knows perfectly well that money spent in the construction of houses finds its way into so many industries that it is one of the best ways in which money can be spent.
If you will proceed to an examination of the report you will find on page after page many suggestions and conclusions on the part of the commission. I find one that deals with land settlement. In my opinion, here again is a very prolific source of assistance to a solution of the problem. They suggest that there be a survey of unoccupied lands and a careful selection of persons eligible for assistance.

Relief and Agricultural Distress
They suggest that a survey be made of improved lands available for settlement and that financial assistance be accorded settlers wishing to move from poorer districts, and so on. Something is being done in that regard now, and I am willing to give the Minister of Agriculture credit along this line. But we are not moving along national lines; that is the point I am impressing upon the house. Turn over the page and you will find suggestions along other lines. For instance, on page 18 I find some conclusions dealing with the way in which the commission recommend that the government should proceed. There is no evidence in any of these measures that the government has even taken notice of these matters. And so on through the report. In many parts of the report numerous suggestions have been made which are not reflected in the legislation before us, and to my mind it is a lamentable thing that this should be so.
I wish now to make one or two general observations. There is nothing wrong with Canada. I have no sympathy whatever for the calamity howlers who tell us the country is going to the bow-wows. The only thing wrong with Canada, as far as I can see, is this: We, the people of Canada-and we who are in parliament must take more responsibility than those outside, because we are in a position of leadership-are not giving leadership to the country. I would put it this way: In the realm of industry I question if those who are the leaders of industry to-day are giving real leadership along the lines of the new economic life that has developed in the industrial realm. I need take only one illustration; it is commonly known, yet nothing is done. In the last few years machinery has displaced literally tens of thousands of workers. That is a platitude; no one Should be entitled to any credit for having said it, but the fact remains that neither the leaders of industry, the leaders of parliament nor the leaders of finance are paying much attention to those hordes of people thrown	out of	work;	nor are	theyattempting to solve the problem of distribution or the social problem that arises therefrom. We know the	situation but	we are doing
next to nothing to face the fact. So I say there is a lack of leadership in the realm of industry.
I think also there is a lack of leadership in the realm of finance, because we find that the outstanding economic phenomenon of modern times	is the	extent	to which	thecontrol of capital has	been	narrowed	into
fewer and fewer hands, by a perfectly natural

process. Publicity; the rapidity of transport and communication between cities and international communications have made it possible for capital to be gathered under the control of smaller and smaller groups. You have your great insurance companies, for instance. I remember that in my boyhood days not very many people had life insurance. To-day it is almost difficult to find anyone who has not life insurance. What does that mean? It means that in the intervening period familiarity with life insurance has increased and the laws concerning it have become so improved that nearly everyone is insured, and that great mass of capital comes under the control of a very small group. I am not saying whether that is bad or good; I am saying dt is a fact. Then take our great banking system, of which we are so jproud. We have a right to be proud of it, because it is one of the most stable banking systems in the world. Here again, however, is there given to the management and control of credit and finance in this country that degree of consideration in regard to public policy that the control of such an immense amount of credit would warrant?
I have given these few illustrations to indicate that there is a lack of leadership, and I had hoped that the government might do something in that regard in view of this report *and the analysis which it contains of the economic conditions of the country, because the report does devote a considerable number of pages to quite an interesting analysis of the economic factors that enter into this problem of unemployment. I had hoped that in view of that report the government might have come before parliament with some leadership in dealing with -these problems. Can we be surprised, as I have said on other occasions, if in a province such as Alberta, for instance, there comes forth a gentleman who leads a certain movement along the line of the control of credit, when he knows that the people of his province, as in many other provinces, are suffering under the pressure of an unbearable debt, personal and public? Should we be surprised if -the people follow someone who at least offers some hope, when other authorities do nothing? That is why I think parliament should have given a great deal more study to these problems than has been given. So I say that in my opinion we have failed lamentably as a parliament; for the moment I shall not speak of the government, which is the leader of parliament and the leader of the country. I will say that parliament, including myself and every member of it, is failing in -this very session, as I think

Relief and Agricultural Distress
we have failed to perhaps a lesser degree in the past, to give leadership in these matters to this country.
These are serious statements, I grant, but they are warranted when we look at the unemployment and distress in this country which is capable of sustaining fifty million people just as easily as not. There is no question about that. We could feed and sustain fifty million people with perfect ease, but what is wrong? In the short time at my disposal I am not prepared to analyse all that is wrong, but we know that certain things are wrong and it is our duty as leaders- every member I see before me is a leader in his community-to find a solution to these problems.
I have already referred to the matter of Canada being capable of sustaining a very much larger population than we have. There is nothing wrong with this country. What I think business men are looking for from the government in the way of leadership is some evidence of stability in business. I think the working classes are looking for security, and I would include, of course, the great agricultural community. They are looking for some degree of security, and as the referee between conflicting industrial, economic and social groups in this country it is our duty as a parliament to see that the game is played fairly, but we are paying little or no attention to it. This measure before the house to-day, which ought to have given the people of this country hope; which ought at least to have given effect to the suggestions contained in the report, is simply a repetition of the acts which we passed in 1936 and 1937, as the minister said when he introduced the bill. I thought that was perhaps one of the most lamentable admissions of defeat to which we could possibly have listened; in the few words with which the minister introduced his bill he said that it did not differ in any essential degree from the acts of last year and the year before, and that is perfectly true. But the minister has had training in these matters; he is young and virile, and when he came to parliament his friends and others looked to him for leadership in this very realm. Can he sit complacently in his seat and feel that by the introduction of the bill that is before us this afternoon he has discharged his duty? I am sorry that I have had to express myself on this matter in strong terms, but I feel that unless we protest vigorously against this inertia, this evasion of responsibility, there is not much chance of stirring either the government or parliament to the action necessary to meet the situation.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, when the minister presented the resolution preceding this bill I did not take part in the discussion; I preferred to wait until the bill was brought down in order to see what he had to offer to the thousands and thousands of unemployed in this country. I happen to be one of those who represent ridings which contain great numbers of people. Unfortunately, altogether too many thousands of the people in my riding are unemployed, and naturally it is my duty to present to this house what I believe to be their hopes in regard to obtaining employment. I want to tell the minister in the kindliest way possible, because I am one of those who have a very high regard for him, that I am tremendously disappointed in this bill. As one who has been associated with labour and employment problems, to the extent of employing thousands of men, I confess I can see very little in the measure which would give employment to those thousands of men who are unemployed. Possibly the minister intends to bring down another resolution or another bill which will indicate what is to be done.

A representative national commission to administer unemployment relief and provide work, and a national system of unemployment insurance.
A commission has been set up-we are commissioned to death, as I have said before, and as I am sorry to say again. But despite that fact, much work has not been provided.

I see one or two rays of hope in the bill from which I would hope some results might come. Yes; but I believe
the government could go ahead and implement the recommendations in the bill which have to do with assistance to industry. That has been done in other countries. Quite true. They may
not have attacked the problem in the proper way. But I hope our minister will do it properly, and I am going to suggest to him a way in which industry can be assisted. We know that industry is being materially assisted in France, thoroughly assisted in Germany, and tremendously assisted in the old country.
I do not know whether or not the minister had the privilege of being in the old country last year; but I had that privilege, and while there I made a thorough survey into the assistance given industry by the British government. I was able to take note of the benefits derived in industrial areas, and I am pleased and happy to say that I found tremendous industrial activity. If the clause in the bill involves an assistance to industry anything like that which I have in mind, or that which has been done elsewhere, well and good.
During the course of a survey I made, I found some information with respect to a factory in Canada, the name of which I should not give, but whose circular I have before me. It is a large industrial institution in Toronto. I am happy to say there is a similar plant in Quebec, one which reflects great credit on our compatriots in that province. Those two companies are now manufacturing in Canada a large piece of equipment for the crushing of stone and the screening of it in one operation. A representative of one of these companies interviewed me in reference to obtaining consideration from the government to assist in the production of these machines. I asked them to what extent the assistance would be required. I was told that blue-prints had been brought in from the United States; that 
Canadian engineers have made thorough surveys of them; that Canadian draftsmen have prepared plans, and that Canadian technicians, toolmakers, engineers, machinists and other workmen have been successful in producing the equipment to manufacture these machines in Canada, one company in Quebec and one in Toronto.

speechtext:
Developing that point
farther, may I say that there are thousands of pieces of equipment now imported which could be made in Canada, in the same way as the machines about which I have been speaking are now being made. In the making of that equipment many thousands of men would be given employment in all walks of activity in industrial institutions. The hon. member has said that machines put men out of work. I do not dispute that fact. But when the machines have to be made, and are imported, I would much sooner have them made by Canadians in Canadian plants than have them made in United States plants by workmen of that country.
If that is part of the minister's proposal, then I will say it is a good one. They have followed that procedure in England. If the minister had been in London last summer, and had visited the industrial areas at Slough and South Wimbledon, he would have seen large numbers of new factories. Some of those are branch factories. I visited one which was a branch of a factory in Toronto, which manufactured steam traps. Those articles are now being made in England, because

the English government saw to it that before the industry received the benefit of the industrial support given by the government, the industry must manufacture to the extent of fifty per cent in England. I found in the plant about seventy-five men who were engaged in the manufacture of steam traps of one kind or another. I inquired of the manager where they were shipping the material and he replied that a great deal of it was sold in England, and that a certain portion went to the Scandinavian countries and to Germany.
That equipment was formerly made in Canada. Why cannot we take a leaf out of the book of the ministries of industry and boards of trade-some are ministries and some are boards of trade-of other countries, where industry is assisted. I had hoped in reading the bill that an attempt was to be made to assist industry, and I said to myself, "There is one thing I can support, even if there is no good in a lot of it." I shall go farther, and say this: I cannot name one line of industry which does not benefit agriculture. Last June Sir Harold Hartley delivered a most enlightening speech at Southport, near London. The subject of his speech was "Agriculture as a potential source of raw materials for industry." That seemed to me to be an extremely good subject and I took particular pains to study what Sir Harold had said. He was dealing with the automobile industry only. He was dealing only with Ford cars manufactured in the United States and the figures he gave had reference to a unit of a million cars. He stated that to manufacture this number of cars, 89,000,000 pounds of cotton were necessary, which represented the production from
558.000	acres of land. Cotton is not grown in Canada, but there are other commodities produced here and other lines of industry to which these figures would apply. I am simply giving the figures that apply to the manufacture of cars in the United States. This consumption is a direct benefit to agriculture in the United States. The cotton was used for upholstering, for the production of brake linings, timing gears, safety glass and so forth.
Half a million bushels of maize-I assume he means corn-were required, representing the production from 11,280 acres, for rubber substitutes, butyl alcohol and other solvents. Next, 2,400,000 pounds of linseed oil, representing the production from 17,500 acres of flax, were required for paints, core oil, soft soap, glycerine, et cetera. The next item is 1,000,000 pounds of lard, the production from 20,000 hogs, for lubricants, brushes, etc. I do not want to get down to the narrow view of this problem; I want to see something done for the working men and women, of whom I have
45.000	in my riding. The next item is 350,000 pounds of mohair, the production from 87,000 goats, for fabrics and upholstering. I do not know where these goats would be raised. It is suggested to me by an hon, member that there are some in the House of Commons, but I doubt that very much. The next item is 2,000,000 pounds of soya bean oil, representing the production from 10,000 acres, used for enamels.
Some hon. members have tried to interject some levity into the discussion of this very serious problem of unemployment. I cannot go home to my riding without the verandah of my house being crowded with people who come to see me to ask if something cannot be done to relieve unemployment. If the minister desires to assist industry, a golden opportunity is given him at the present time. Earlier in the session I made reference to what I had heard during my visits to munition, steel and gun plants in the United Kingdom. I suggested that the government get in touch with the British government in order to encourage the removal of some of these great plants to Canada. One of the ministers, I have forgotten just which one, laughed at the idea. However, during the last few days there have been reports in the newspapers about the suggested manufacture in this country of airplanes for war purposes. According to press reports the British commissioners are now in the United States and the suggestion has been made that seven, eight, or perhaps ten thousand airplanes will be manufactured. I am giving an arbitrary figure; the actual figure may be less. I for one would like to see these airplanes made in the great plants of this country. Every thousand men put to work making airplanes would be a thousand less to provide for in connection with unemployment relief and an increased home market

would be provided for our Canadian farmers. I hope the minister will do everything he can to encourage the production of airplanes in this country.
There are other industries that might be encouraged to come over here. Any one who knows anything about the industrial areas realizes how congested they are. Slough, South Wimbleton, Port Talbot, Manchester and other areas are all extremely congested. If these areas were destroyed, it might prove difficult for the British government to carry on a war. If these industries were moved to Canada, they would be two or three thousand miles further away from possible attack by bombing planes.
I had hoped that something would be in this bill about the proposals which have been submitted by the Ontario government to this government with reference to flood prevention; that we would have heard something about the proposals of the Ontario government to eliminate floods on the Grand river. The hon. member for Brantford City (Mr. Macdonald), a very capable member of this house, exceptionally capable when he gets up and gives a good tariff protection speech for the industries and industrial workers of that great industrial city of Brantford-and when he does that we are ready to welcome him over here for he is fighting for the working men of Brantford-after he had interviewed a number of the ministers of the cabinet, said:
While I cannot say definitely what action the government will take I am satisfied that the commissioners convinced the three members of the cabinet that the scheme was one that was needed.
If the minister would assist the Ontario government in commencing that great scheme of flood prevention and would commence with the Grand river; then if the government receives any commendation from the public, I would say more power to its elbow as long as it is doing its duty, and I am satisfied that in preventing floods on the Grand river it would be doing good work. That is only one river, but what would it mean in connection with the Grand river alone?
The area of the Grand river north of Galt, which is in the riding represented by the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Edwards) is 1,360 square miles. Apparently, in submitting their figures to the minister, the Ontario government used the identical figures I used a year ago as to the cost of water conservation on the Grand river. I do not say that they used my figures, but their figures are identical with mine. I had estimated, on the records of a water conserva-

Relief and Agricultural Distress
tion survey, that the cost would be approximately $2,000,000; I am not sure that $2,000,000 would do it; but the Ontario government, after no doubt going into the matter carefully, have come to the same conclusion. Their figures would likely be based on what was generally accepted as the standard when floods are bad, that is a three-day rain flood. A three-day flood would cover the whole of that area on that basis, if the water remained on the land to a depth of approximately 2-75 inches, and during the course of such flood about 8,700,000,000 cubic feet of water would fall. To provide for the retention of surplus water so that it would not cause damage at Brantford and the other towns on the banks of the river would create work for 3,700 men for four months, who would be directly engaged in the work of conservation, and I am satisfied that it would provide work also for another 3,700 men making the cement and steel and all the other materials and equipment entering into the construction of the necessary conservation works. If the minister has anything like that in mind, I say more power to his elbow. After having tested it out on the Grand river, if he finds it satisfactory, he could extend the operations to the other rivers which are in flood every year all over this country. Everyone has read of them during the last few years. I shall read only a few headlines on articles describing these floods: "Port Hope facing acute situation from flood waters"- "Port Hope faces its fifth flood this winter"- "Waterloo in danger"-"Galt main street under water." One town after another along the banks of the Grand river was in danger from floods. The same thing occurred with the Thames river. It was not the case so much with the Saugeen, but the same thing happened along the Kettle river which flows through St. Thomas and down into lake Erie. There was a flood there last spring which caused a good deal of trouble.
I believe there is a real opportunity for the sound investment of money and the providing of a lot of employment. Every one of these floods causes not only deaths as a rule but a lot of property damage, and any money which this government invests for the purpose of eliminating property damage necessarily does not cost the country anything. I do not know where you would get the money, but I am sure, if the minister directs that these works shall be done, the money will be found to do it.
There is another way in which money can be spent as a national investment, not as a matter of cost at all, and that is in the construction of good roads. I may be asked
where the money would come from to do that. Money can always be found for a real investment, and money spent on good roads is a national investment. Last summer-I dislike referring to thjg because I do not like talking about things I have seen, except that one can always explain better something that he has seen than something he has read of -I made a little survey of road-building in Germany, and I saw their new concrete roads with eight lanes, accommodating four cars on each side of a boulevard, and with concrete so thick that the heavy tanks of the German army can speed over them at sixty miles an hour. I am not asking this government to provide roads over which tanks can speed at sixty miles an hour. We want to be free from tanks in this Country. We hope that war will never occur. But what did road-building do for Germany? Just what did it mean to Germany last year? It is almost incredible but nevertheless a fact that road-building in Germany in a single year resulted in the removal of earth from the roadways on which concrete was later to be poured of a greater quantity than was removed in the building of the Panama canal. In building the Panama canal the United States engineers removed 220,000,000 cubic metres of earth. In building the roadways of Germany last year, the brawn of German youth removed 250,000.000 cubic metres of earth, so that the concrete could be poured. Subsequently they poured 10,000,000 cubic metres of concrete, and it took 260,000 cars to deliver the concrete. So in doing that work Germany did go a long way towards relieving or eliminating unemployment. In fact, I did not see an able-bodied young man on the streets of Berlin between the ages of 16 and 20. A lot of them were probably in camps, and a lot in the army and navy, but a lot of them were making roads. One of the ministers with whom I discussed roadbuilding told me that they had hundreds of thousands of their young men engaged in building roads.
In this country we have been giving the dole and little else to our young men. A young man does not want the dole. He wants work, and if he gets work building a road, and receives fair wages for doing it, he is giving the best possible return to the country because good roads are a national asset, and if road-building is in the minister's program I am behind it one hundred per cent. If the minister will support the province of Ontario in building really good roads, going the shortest distance between two points, he

Relief and Agricultural Distress
will be helping to create a national asset and do a great deal in the way of providing employment.
I do not know that there is much more that I can say. I had no intention of speaking at any length. The hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) mentioned housing. Let me mention just one example of housing that I saw last summer, to illustrate the fine work which this country can do in improving housing conditions in this country. If the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar), under whose jurisdiction the Indian department is, I believe, were in the house, he might be interested in what I am going to say. I have made a survey of many Indian reserves, but I have particularly in mind the Muncey reserve, west of London. I doubt if anybody who has not been there could believe that the conditions on that reserve are as they are. I went to one residence occupied by an Indian; I had a letter from him to-day. It was a hut, if I remember correctly, nine feet wide by twelve feet long. I could see out of every corner of it. In many places the rain could come through the roof. In the hut were two small bunks, not beds; that was the accommodation for the Indian, his wife and his four children. The day I was there his daughter, one of the four children I referred to, had returned from the Indian school, which I assume is at Muncey; it is not far from the mounted police headquarters. At that school the young woman had been taught all that white children are taught; she had received the tuition to make her an educated young lady; she had reached the age when she had to leave the school, and she returned to this hut nine feet by twelve, where you could see out of every corner and the rain could come through the roof in several places, and where there were just two bunks. The Indians were the original owners of this country. It may be that they are not entitled to any consideration through a building program; but we all know that whites require such a program, and that the aborigine, not being able now to defend and provide for himself, requires our help. I saw several huts on that reservation and other reservations where conditions are no better than in the one I have described, and I contend that conditions like that should not be allowed in any civilized country, whether the sufferer be a white man or an aborigine.
Although I intended to speak on this bill, I was unable to find time to prepare much to say because my tame yesterday was taken up with a delegation from Toronto, including

a returned soldier. The returned soldier had been a prisoner of war in Germany for three years. He with six of his comrades had been captured while they had been hiding in a dug-out. The division to which they belonged had been surrounded; the German army had gone away beyond their position, but in searching through the trenches some Germans came upon these men and threatened to bomb them unless they came out. The Germans, being three in number, decided that six prisoners were too many for them to take away, and were discussing whether they should shoot them when an officer came along and said "no shooting," as a German says it, and the six men were saved. That poor fellow was here yesterday trying to get some adjustment of his pension. Before he came here, so that I could make myself conversant with his circumstances and what he was up against, I visited his little cottage on Salem avenue, Toronto. I venture to say there was not more than fifty dollars' worth of furniture in the cottage. How anybody lives in it I do not know. I am sorry that such conditions are allowed in Toronto; but doubtless there are many such cases, and the municipal authorities, there as in the great city of Montreal, have a heavy task. If the minister intends to proceed with any housing scheme, such conditions would warrant and certainly would require almost any amount of money that he is willing to spend. As an hon. member remarked a few minutes ago, it is the lack of building more than anything else that is holding things back in this country. It may not be economic to spend a large amount of money; but if the cabinet, knowing the situation as they do, undertake to spend a substantial amount to provide cheaper and better homes for the average worker, they will receive unstinted praise, and the minister likewise.
That is all I can say at this time. I did not rise in any spirit of criticism, but rather I wanted to try to encourage the minister to go the limit towards providing employment for the unemployed in this country.

I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) upon the excellent sequel he gave to his previous address on the resolution upon which this bill is based. This is the second reading, on which we are asked to agree to the principle of the bill. The social credit group, to which I belong, are not opposed to the principle of this bill; but we are opposed to this government's attitude of defeat concerning the underlying cause of the break-down in our

Questions
economic system, of which this unemployment problem is simply an evidence. We are asked to agree to the principle of this bill, and since there is nothing better offered us we must agree to it. At the same time we are being asked to agree-against which I protest-to the principle of distributing money to people in the most morale-destroying, self-respect-destroying method yet devised by man. The group with which I am associated are heartily opposed to that. I am sure that the government itself must also be opposed to it.
Rather than let people starve, since there is no alternative, and since the people who are to receive the benefit have appetites, come by just as honestly as mine or any other hon. member's, I would urge the early passage of the bill. I have not referred particularly to that part of the bill which deals with agricultural distress, because agriculture is only one of our industries. But I should like to point out to the house and the government, that an adequate economic system would absorb automatically the consequences of such unavoidable natural failures, without the degradation of relief. I submit that the government should be bending every possible effort towards accomplishing that purpose.

Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:	1
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to provide for the refunding of matured, maturing and callable financial obligations of the Canadian National Railways and for the issue of securities guaranteed by the Dominion of Canada in respect of such refunding to an aggregate principal amount not exceeding $200,000,000.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext:
The legislation now on
the statute book with respect to the refunding of Canadian National obligations was enacted in 1935. It was for the same sum as will be embodied in the bill which will be founded on this resolution. The amount of the authority remaining is just over $6,000,000, and therefore it is essential to have further authority to deal with these maturing and callable obligations of the Canadian National.
I may say that under the authority of the last act the refunding which has been accomplished resulted in an annual saving in interest charges of approximately $3,900,000. I think that is all I need say at this stage, unless someone wants specific information with respect to any particular issue. I shall be prepared, both now and during the different stages of the bill, to answer any questions regarding the refunding which has occurred.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I thought possibly the minister might give us a list at this stage of the refundings that have been made. I was also going to ask him whether any steps had been taken, and if so what, with respect to the perpetual high rate of interest obligations, both of the old Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Railway. I realize that with respect to the Grand Trunk we are under obligation to pay an annuity in the terms of the interest on the obligations that were taken over when we secured the system, but with respect to the other obligations there is a fine question, which the minister no doubt has considered. We are not guarantors with respect to some of these securities upon which interest is paid and there is a question whether or not this country should place itself in the position of guaranteeing the interest upon these securities. I am sure that this is a matter that has engaged the attention of the minister, as it did of previous ministers. For instance, 
certain of the income certificates were settled by the administration of which the present Minister of Finance was a member. Undoubtedly in that instance we took a course which we were not obliged to take; we assumed financial responsibilities which were not written in the bond. On the other hand there is a question whether we as owners of the properties can escape the payment of the interest. This is a matter in connection with which different opinions have been held from time to time by various people. I am expressing no opinion of my own at the moment because I desire to leave the matter an open question.
I have looked at the report a great many times in my lifetime and I have looked at it again to see whether or not these six per cent perpetual securities, for instance, might be retirsd. There may be a question whether or not this can be done on terms that would be sound financially, because many of these securities are not on the market and to buy them would mean having to pay a high price. Then if you bought them at a high premium you would not be making any money if you substituted for them a low interest rate security. In the main it is fair to say that the securities have been selling on the basis of the present rate for money, and therefore nothing would be gained by it. That is one of the difficulties the minister has to consider. If he has any information on the subject I think this would be a very appropriate time to give it to the committee.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS

The matters to which the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) has referred have of course engaged the attention not only of this government but of at least three of its predecessors, and I think every government has worked out the particular problem which could be dealt with during its period of office to the best advantage of the Dominion of Canada, having regard to the circumstances of the time.
There is one issue of perpetuals, four per cents, which is now callable. Obviously the only question there is one of judgment as to when and under what conditions to take advantage of the call privilege.

speechtext:
Perhaps the minister
would, between now and when the bill is in committee, look into the following questions and have answers for them.
On page 19 of the Canadian National Railways report there is reference made to five perpetual issues of the Grand Trunk Railway. I should like to know whether any of them are callable, and if so, when and on what terms. I have a fair memory with respect to some of them, but the question often arises and I think it might be desirable to have the information on Hansard to show that some of these cannot be dealt with by any government, however much it might desire to deal with them, in the absence of agreement on the part of the holders to have them dealt with. The five per cent stock we assumed responsibility for as a term of the transfer of the Grand Trunk to this country, and I apprehend that very little can be done with respect to it.
On page 20 of the annual report there are certain issues under the title, "Other issues," four of which are perpetual four per cents, some Canadian Northern, some Canadian Northern Ontario, some Canadian Northern
Quebec, and some Quebec and Lake St. John Railway. In addition to that, there is an issue of Grand Trunk six per cent third preference bonds, but the issue is so very small that possibly it could not bear the expense of considering it, except that it is an eyesore to see it there. It is only $70,000. Perhaps the minister would also give us that information before we come to deal with the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: Yes.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext:
There arises the other question which is constantly before the minister, and that is the guarantee given by the provinces. We have never released the provinces from their obligations, but in point of fact when Saskatchewan and Alberta were called upon to make payments we did repay them the money they paid. That is true in both cases. Now the obligations that mature at a not too distant date with respect to these provinces would seem to me to afford an opportunity to the federal government to treat them as a factor in dealing with the financial situation between the dominion and the provinces; because undoubtedly what we
C.NJt.-R e funding

have done is to relieve the provinces of a burden that would have absolutely involved bankruptcy on their part had they been called upon to make payment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: Do not confine it to those two provinces alone.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: No, the western provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: We have assumed liability with respect to all the provinces.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext:
No, not assumed.; we
have not called upon the provinces to pay. The point I am trying to make, and it should be kept constantly in mind, is that there has been no assumption on our part of liability.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: Quite. But no province has been called upon to pay.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: That is the point I am making. We have assumed no responsibility but the company has discharged the liability with money Obtained from the federal exchequer from year to year. That is, the guarantee by the province has not been implemented, nor has any request been made to implement it, but the interest charges on the securities guaranteed by the provinces have been treated as a general continuing obligation of the system and paid for accordingly, whether it is part of the deficit or-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: That is true of all provinces save two.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: I did not know there were two, because I did not know that the earnings of the Canadian Northern Ontario were sufficient to enable it to pay its obligations.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext:
I was thinking only of
those provinces which gave no guarantees. They are, I think, Quebec and New Brunswick-no, Prince Edward Island.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext:
New Brunswick did
give a guarantee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: There is only one province, then, Prince Edward Island, which did not give a guarantee.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: That is the only one of which I have any knowledge. Under those circumstances possibly the minister may be able to give us a clear statement when the bill is in committee, indicating just what the provincial obligations are. The great bond companies have issued a pamphlet every year giving that information very fully, but I think that for the purpose of having it on Hansard as a permanent memorial for the benefit of all members of the house-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: "Memorial" is good.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: Yes, "memorial" is good, -it may be very desirable that the minister should make that statement; and any comments I desire to make on the matter can be made later.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: Of course the information referred to is in the annual report of the railway, but if my right hon. friend would like it on Hansard I shall see that it is placed there when the bill is in committee. In the meantime I can give some general information to the hon. member for Dan-forth (Mr. Harris) with respect to guaranteed and unguaranteed-that is in bulk. In 1937 the funded debt of the Canadian National Railways outstanding in the hands of the public consisted of $970,697,190 guaranteed by the government of Canada and $251,030,209 either guaranteed by provinces or entirely unguaranteed. At the moment I have not the figures separated as between the amounts guaranteed by provinces and the amounts unguaranteed by any government; but that, at all events, will be a piece of the information for which my right hon. friend is looking.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: If, as I understood it was remarked by the right hon. leader of the opposition that we cannot deal with these perpetual bonds unless we can get the holders of them to agree to give them up, I at least should like to express my dissent from- that position. I believe that under our powers to legislate with regard to railways, we can provide that they shall be callable at a date we fix, and if we fix the date at say five years from now, we could call them at that time. There is another way in which certainly they could be dealt with-a similar suggestion has been made by the leader in Saskatchewan of the party to which the right hon gentleman belongs, so I assume he would not quarrel with it-namely, that all interest over and above three per cent per annum should be taxed back again by this country. I suggest to the Minister of Finance that he consider one or the other proposition; and I also ask him to place on Hansard, if he will do so, a statement of these so-called perpetual debentures and the rates of interest which they bear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: That will be included in the statement.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext:
That is what I understood. I see that the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) is not quite appreciative of what I said. I did not say that you would have to deal with all of them, because some of them are callable, but I did point out what is the main thing, to be found at page 19 of the report of the company, namely that the

C.N.R.-R e funding
perpetual obligations of the Grand Trunk Railway issued from, 1875 to 1883 were assumed by this country as a part of the purchase price of 'the Grand Trunk Railway-which is an entirely different condition from that to which reference has been made. The bargain by which we got that railway was to pay to the people who 'held those securities the interest on them in accordance with the terms of the securities themselves. It will be recalled that when the arbitration was before the court the evidence indicated that we made an additional offer, which they declined, which would have given them something for the common stock-which the tribunal found was worth nothing. It is not a question of our dealing with them; it is a question of their having been given an underbaking by us that we would pay a rental-it amounts to that- in the form of interest payments on perpetual securities to the holders thereof for taking over the railway from them, which we did by statute. That is an entirely different thing from the issue of an ordinary perpetual security by a railway with respect to which we have assumed obligations to service, but which might be dealt with by many methods if we so desired.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: I fail to see why, when we made an agreement that now is proving unconscionable from the standpoint of the people of this county-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: We did not make an agreement.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext:
-it can be said that we cannot do anything unless we get the other party to agree. Obviously it would be found that people who hold agreements like that are none too ready to give up the rights they have; but I do sincerely suggest that we should deal with this question at once. When this country is now paying six per cent on an obligation which is outstanding-I do not care how it arose in the past

it should be dealt with without any further delay. These obligations could be made callable at any period in the future; I would suggest a period of five years. If that is not deemed the best way to deal with it, the other proposition should be considered; anybody who has an income in this country is subject to be taxed. These people got an agreement which is a little too good to those who benefit by it, and I suggest that to tax people on income from bonds bearing a rate of over and above three per cent is a fair way of dealing with the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: Lest there should be an impression go abroad which in my judgment would be harmful to Canada, I must dissent from a suggestion of any intention on the part of this government to do anything which would involve the breaking of the pledged word of the Dominion of Canada. I want that distinctly understood. At the same time I deprecate discussion of this kind because of the fact that it does hinder bona fide negotiations between parties who may mutually desire to make an arrangement; I mean, by debtors and creditors sitting down together and working out their problems. So far as this dominion is concerned, to have any idea go out from these halls that we were contemplating deliberately breaking our word, either directly or by any device, could not possibly do any of the population of Canada any good and certainly would do the dominion as a whole a great deal of hianm.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: I take issue with the suggestion that if you 'tax an income that is probably unfair from the standpoint of the body politic-and I submit that six per cent on a government obligation is unfair from the standpoint of the people of this country- you are breaking your agreement with anybody.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: I did not intend to imply any such thing. As is well known to all hon. members, we do tax income at the present time. There is no question about that. But if I understood the hon. member correctly, his suggestion was that we single out this particular income and tax it on a scale that we are not taxing other income of a similar kind. If that is the method suggested, then obviously it is an indirect method of getting out of an obligation for which we might otherwise be liable, and I deprecate any idea going abroad that any government of Canada would contemplate breaking directly or indirectly the pledged word of the country.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext:
I understood the minister to say that the dominion had never released the provinces from what I might call the original liability of the provinces, although the dominion had taken over these bonds in actual fact and had paid the interest on them many years ago. As far as British Columbia is concerned we have always understood there that there was a distinct arrangement, that the dominion had absolutely released the province from their liability under the bonds; [DOT]the quid pro quo being that the province released the dominion from the obligation of the railway company to build a line from, I think, the neighbourhood of Red pass down
C.N.R.-Refunding

to Vancouver, and agreed that the Canadian National Railway should use their own line instead of building this extension demanded under the bond, so to speak.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: I have no recollection of any release at any time of any province with respect to its original liability under its provincial guarantee. I shall be pleased, however, to verify that between now and the time the bill is before the house.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext:
This matter was before the special committee which has been sitting these last few days. As a member of that committee I said something about the interest which we found was payable on these perpetual bonds, and lest I may be misunderstood as more or less acquiescing in the opinion that we should continue to pay this interest I want to make this statement.
I quite agree with the Minister of Finance that this country should do nothing which would affect the general credit of Canada. At the same time we must recognize that these bonds that we took over were originally not between this government and certain people but between the Grand Trunk Railway and those people. Had we allowed the Grand Trunk Railway to go into bankruptcy, as it undoubtedly would have done had the country not stepped in and taken it over, the holders of the bonds would undoubtedly have suffered. In my opinion an interest rate of six per cent cannot be justified, and I would sincerely ask the Minister of Finance to explore every reasonable avenue to see that the burden of this very high interest rate is in some way removed from the shoulders of the Canadian National system and the people of Canada.

It is unfortunate that this question should have come up without any notice. I do not blame the minister, but had notice been given of it there is a phase of the subject that I should like to have discussed. However, I will take it up when the bill is under consideration.
Considerable reference has been made to the possibility of negotiation for better terms in connection with these bonds, and reference has also been made to the arbitration and the Grand Trunk purchase by the dominion. I believe the statement was made that there had been an offer to the Grand Trunk shareholders which they rejected. I am informed, however, that those who were particularly concerned, and who ultimately suffer, did not have a proper or legal opportunity to vote upon the question whether or not that offer should have been accepted. This bill, when

it comes in, will probably afford the minister a chance for negotiation in connection with these very much disputed claims.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS

In any case the annual

I was pleased to learn that
the minister was exploring every possible avenue in an attempt to reduce the interest load on the Canadian National railway system. I notice that by the refunding of the present loan approximately S3,000,000 is to be saved.

speechtext: I remember there was a loan of approximately that amount bearing an interest rate of six and a half per cent. I do not think that any government guaranteed loan ought to bear an interest rate of six and a half per cent. It is far too high. The minister will recognize that. Personally I should like to see the Department of Finance use every means at their disposal in an effort to get the interest structure down to a level where there shall be no outstanding loans at more than three per cent per annum. That is a fair rate to pay. When we begin discussing questions of economy in connection with the railways, that is the first place where in my opinion economies should be effected.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: I have no desire to discuss this question to-day or to do anything that would embarrass the minister in his negotiations, but when he suggests that anyone who makes a plea for a change in existing arrangements is guilty of urging the government to break its pledged word.-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext:
-then I challenge that statement. I do not like that high moral tone assumed in the ease of perpetual bonds while on the other hand the people of Canada are allowed to suffer under an injustice simply because someone speaking for the government
years ago committed this country to certain obligations-call it obligations if you like- that were unjust and unwarranted. It does not seem to me that we should take the ground that simply because certain legal obligations were incurred at that time there is no way of getting out of the difficulty. A good many people are suggesting that some way must be found-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: I agree with that.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: -^and I do not think that we ought to be told that we are immoral-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: I must take exception to that; I never used such a word-

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: I know the minister did not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: -nor did I intend to convey any such implication. So far as I am concerned the imputation should be withdrawn.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: I gladly withdraw it. But the minister took very high moral ground when he said that we must maintain our honourable obligations, and so on. That is hardly fair in a matter of this kind. We should not have had perpetual bonds. No one should be permitted, in the name of the country, to put this country under tribute as it is under tribute to-day. There are certain ways of adjusting these debts on a fair basis. We have had examples in the west, under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, in which very definite changes in arrangements have been made. If it could be done with the small mortgage holder it can be done with the larger mortgage holders that we call bondholders, whether resident in this country or outside.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: Does my hon. friend suggest that we should put the railways into bankruptcy?

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: The railways should have been put into bankruptcy many years ago, before they were taken over.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: That may be so, but in order to make a parallel with the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, bankruptcy proceedings are involved.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext:
I am not suggesting that it is an exact parallel, but I do suggest that it is one instance in which the people of this country, finding themselves in an impossible position, discovered a way out, and we shall have to do something of the kind in connection with the railway debt. There have been revolutions in other countries; why? Simply because there seemed to be no legal
C.N.R.-Refunding

way of getting justice. Not very long ago Mexico seized the holdings of the great oil companies and then the government began to negotiate with regard to what compensation should be paid. This has gone on the world over. Violent revolution, or illegal seizure, if you like to call it "illegal" has come simply because of the breakdown of constitutional and legal ways of dealing with realities. We have a right to urge that the people of Canada should not be called upon any longer to pay a tribute of this magnitude. I feel quite confident that if the ground is strongly taken-and it is a reasonable ground-that some way out must be found, then some way will be found. The minister may deplore the use of indirect means. I do not much care whether the means are direct or indirect, but we have to find a way of easing the burden under which the people are now labouring.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: One further word, lest an impression should go abroad throughout Canada that the Canadian railway debt carries a very high rate of interest. The matters which are now under discussion represent a portion only, and a relatively small portion, of the Canadian National indebtedness. It is well for the people of Canada to know that the average rate of interest being paid to-day on the total indebtedness of the Canadian National Railways approximates four per cent. I say that lest there should be an idea that we are paying six or seven per cent on vast sums of money. But that does not lessen the necessity for any government to do everything it honourably can to reduce the interest burden. I again use the word "honourably." If the government is not the seat of honour, where are we going? I make no apologies for saying that the government should go as far as it can go honourably in making arrangements to eliminate excessive interest rates wherever they exist. I do not take second place even to my hon. friend in that regard. But I believe that the good of the people of Canada is best served by keeping their pledged word, and negotiating within that limit. I do not believe that the example of Mexico or other places is a good example for Canada.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: The minister has just repeated the kind of statement to which I rose to object. If we advocate some other policy it is not because we are any more lacking in honour than the minister-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: Quite right.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext:
I say that very distinctly. In a few minutes we shall come to the discussion of unemployment in this

country, and knowing as I do of thousands of young men to-day who have no chance whatever in life, some of them being driven to lives of crime by the necessitous circumstances in which they find themselves, and knowing that this government is not living up to its pledged word on which it was elected to power, I want the minister to be very careful in claiming any higher degree of honour than the rest of us in this house.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext:
My hon. friend is too
adroit for me. I did not claim any higher degree of honour than anyone else; I was speaking, not of my honour or the honour of my hon. friend, but of the word of the Dominion of Canada, pledged by Canada's duly authorized representatives at any particular time. If it will please my hon. friend, I doulbt whether my own standard of honour would equal his.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: It is not a matter of personal honour; I was not in any way reflecting on the minister's personal honour. But I do protest against the conception, which is very prevalent, that a government's pledged word to one class of people is superior to the government's pledged word to another class. Take the example of a returned man who met me yesterday, asking for a hand-out. When the government asked men to go overseas and risk their lives in the service of this country it pledged its honour to care for them on their return. And I am not saying that the government has not done a great deal. But there are scores of those poor fellows to-day who have no opportunity of living a decent life. I admit that this is all part of a very involved question but I take this opportunity of urging upon the government that the care of people of that kind is just as much' a debt of honour as the carrying out of the terms of any financial document to which the government has placed its signature.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: It is a more important debt. We may differ as to the manner of dealing with some things, but we do not differ as to the relative importance of those debts.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: I am glad to hear that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: Unquestionably the debt of the people of Canada, as represented by their government, to humanity comes first; there is no question about that. My hon. friend cannot put us in that position.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext:
It has been so treated by all governments.
