speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext:
It has been so treated
by successive governments.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: Oh, no.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext:
In regard to the point taken by the Minister of Finance that there is something wrong about a special tax, I do not think there is anything wrong about a special tax if such is necessary to do justice. The Minister of Finance introduced such a bill since I have been a member of this house. At the time the civil servants had their pay reduced by ten per cent it was regarded as a breach of the country's obligation to reduce the salaries of judges, of military officers and of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police; accordingly a special tax of ten per cent was .placed upon their incomes. I suggest it will be no more unfair to place a special tax on the holders of these railway bonds to reduce their rate of interest to a reasonable rate.
I suggest that something should be dome in this resolution to give power to deal with these bonds. The wording of the resolution is:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to provide for the refunding of matured, maturing and callable financial obligations of the Canadian National Railways. . . .
I assume that these obligations which are under discussion, these so-called perpetuals, are neither matured, maturing nor callable and so are not covered by the resolution. I suggest that the government should deal with these without further delay, and that power should be taken to deal with that type of obligation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: There is no question about our having power to negotiate. The government have power to negotiate with respect to any matter.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext:
It may be a delicate matter for a farmer to venture into the realm of finance, but I could not sit here representing a part of this dominion without taking the opportunity to state here as not only my opinion but that of my people back home that we should not fail to take advantage of every chance that occurs for refunding these obligations at a lower rate of interest. I do not think there is an hon. member in the chamber who does not believe in his heart that that is long overdue. When we look back and see the hardships that the people have suffered on account of these high interest rates, the homes that they have lost, the children's educations which have been sacrificed, we are reminded that the people of Canada have kept on paying this interest through all this time of turmoil and stress.
The Minister of Finance knows well that Canadian National bonds bearing as high as seven per cent interest were refunded last summer.
I am just as jealous of my word and the word of Canada as any hon. member; but is it imposible for us to make arrangements with the bondholders without violating our pledged word? We have waited many years for the bondholders to take one step towards offering to do this, and they have not offered. I say an arrangement might be made without violating that word, and I will give an example. In 1897 Canada pledged her word and paid four million dollars to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to enable them to build a railway line. In turn the Canadian Pacific pledged their word and signed an agreement to the effect that they would never charge more than a certain rate on commodities coming east, and commodities going west. In 1922 I was a member of the house when, by action of the house, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company were allowed to violate that agreement. Perhaps I should not say "violate"; they were allowed to amend the agreement in such a way that we lost the rate that we had paid for on commodities going west. I give this as an example of one instance where Canada did make an arrangement with a certain company and then changed the agreement. I do not think we violated our word.
I say in all sincerity to the Minister of Finance that I know the troubles he has, but we should seize the opportunity we have here to-day to issue an invitation to bondholders to see if they will not consent to a reduction in their earnings as other people of Canada have had to do.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, has the minister communicated with the holders of perpetual bonds to ascertain their opinions? I know that the province of Alberta wrote letters to the bondholders asking for their cooperation with a view to handling the debt situation in that province, and received no answer. The bondholders of Canada, particularly bondholders in connection with provincial governments, do not wish to cooperate; they do not wish to negotiate with a view to solving the debt problems of the provinces. The same holds true of the municipalities.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext:
The hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) and the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Young) are both under a misapprehension with regard to interest rates. With respect to the six per cent interest, there is only $70,000 of principal outstanding, and the saving of three per cent on that is about
C.N.R.-Refunding

$2,000 a year which is a substantial sum, in one way. There are seven per cent securities outstanding with respect to only $86,000, so that we have with respect to the Canadian National an obligation of $156,000 bearing a higher rate of interest than five per cent. That is point number one
Number two is that this country did not issue those perpetual securities The difficulty is that member after member has suggested that we undertook to issue a perpetual security The only perpetual security which has been issued in this country, so far as I know, was one which was issued a few months ago by the Minister of Finance and is now selling at about 88 or 90.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: A three per cent perpetual, yes.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext:
Yes, and that is the first one this country has issued, so far as I know. The perpetual securities to which reference has been made, and which carry an interest rate beyond three per cent, are perpetual securities issued by the Grand Trunk Railway and the Canadian Northern Railway-that is, the Mackenzie and Mann railway, and the old Grand Trunk. Those companies did issue perpetual securities, the same as the Canadian Pacific Railway four per cent perpetual debenture stock, which, of course, has been sold in the markets of the world, largely in Great Britain. I think practically the whole of these perpetual securities of the Grand Trunk are held in Great Britain, and a great many of them are held in family trusts. But it would not make any difference if that interest rate were reduced to one per cent; it would not save us a dollar

not one dollar- because we have agreed to pay the Grand Trunk the equivalent of that much money. That is the point I wish to make, and that is the whole difficulty.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: And we did that by act of this parliament.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext:
Yes, by statute of this parliament. It is not a question of interest at all; that might all be taken away to-morrow and they would have to get exactly the same sum of money. It is covered by statute.
Reference has been made to what has been done under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. I may say it was the view of the tribunal which considered the question that the Grand Trunk was not insolvent with respect to these securities. That is, it was worth in any event the amount of money that was represented by these securities. Hence it was that the country, instead of going on the market and borrowing, simply undertook to

pay the Grand Trunk a sum of money which serviced these perpetual obligations. And if the rate were two per cent we would still have to pay the same sum of money. This matter has come up without notice, and I will have to give from recollection what knowledge I have of it, because I have not looked it up for years; but that is the position as I understand it. This has nothing to do with common stock. It has no connection, except with these perpetual securities, and I believe this was designated in the statute which dealt with it. That is, it is an annual payment which amounts to sufficient money for the purpose of servicing those perpetual obligations.
There is one other six and a half per cent security outstanding-and I always think the people who bought those securities in New York took advantage of our great difficulty. It was a time when this country was in a tremendously difficult position, and money was demanding a very high price. I was not in the House of Commons at the time of the transaction, but I know we paid six and a half per cent for it, which was an exceedingly high rate. It matures in eight years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: Seven years.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: I say that if you will compare the average interest rates of the National railway system with those of the other great railway systems on the North American continent, you will have reason to feel proud of them. As a matter of fact if you will look at the figures in connection with similar securities in Great Britain you will have good cause to hold up your heads. Leaving out the $70,000 and the $86,000, and the $24,000,000 issue of 1921, all of which pay a rate higher than five per cent, you find that some are two per cent, some are three per cent and some are four per cent, the usual rate that is being paid for these securities. That is the basis of what was to be a very valuable security, especially with respect to perpetual Grand Trunks, for the reason everyone knows, that we have undertaken as a country to pay sufficient money to service those obligations at the rate provided. If we had a rate of one per cent we would still have to pay the same sum of money.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext:
The hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) is a very sincere member, and I am sure he does not wish either here or in the country to give a wrong impression. I am not referring particularly to any observation he made, but rather to the trend of the discussion, and the idea that with respect to their Canadian

C.NJi.-R e funding
National obligations the people of this country are paying an unconscionable rate of interest.
I would like to point out to him that it is my job to work at that problem every day. I have conscientiously endeavoured to do it every minute I have been in office. Some of the results, not only of my work but of that of other men equally conscientious who preceded me, are contained in the public accounts so that he who runs may read. But the people will not read them. In the estimates before the house is a reduction in the interest charge on the public debt of this country amounting to about $5,500,000, as a result of taking advantage of such opportunities as come in connection with money markets and in connection with maturing obligations.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: We saved $14,000,000 on one conversion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext:
I might point out further that it is not a partisan matter. Any man who occupies this position is supposed to give of his brain and experience. He should endeavour to manage the finances of this country in such a way that the load upon the people shall be as light as possible. Any man in this position who does not do that ought not to occupy it. May I point out that in spite of the fact that the public debt of Canada is to-day one billion dollars higher than it was in 1924, the debt charges to-day are just about what they were in that year That is not a testimony to myself alone; it is a testimony to the fact that the men who are serving us in the Department of Finance and the ministers who have sat at this desk have continuously both in and out of season, used their best business and financial judgment in managing the public debt, even though they have not been very successful in preventing its abnormal increase. I want to mark that particularly.
This house votes the increases in public debt. These are probably necessary for any one of a thousand things, particularly during such periods as those through which we have just passed. If the financial management of the country has been such as to take care of a billion dollars of increase in the public debt and it is not costing any more in interest to-day than it did when the debt was a billion dollars less, surely that fact ought to be known by the people of Canada. It should also be known that the average rate at this moment on the Canadian public debt is less than three and a half per cent. I am not speaking by the book, in fact it might be three and a quarter per cent,
but it is somewhere between three and a quarter and three and a half per cent. I would like you to look at the public debts of all the countries of the world and tell me how many of them can show an average debt charge of less than three and a half per cent. Remember we have a high public debt in relation to our population. The body that creates the public debt is this parliament and the financial management of the public debt must be in the hands of the government of the day. I know my hon. friend will say that the initiation of increases in the public debt rests with the government of the day. Of course that is true, but it is also true-

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: Public pressure.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: We all know that there is public pressure behind all of us. As a matter of fact I believe the functions of parliament have changed completely. As originally constituted, parliament was a gathering of the commoners representing the taxpayers to prevent the king from spending too much of their money. Listening to speakers from all sides, it would seem to-day that the character of parliament has been reversed; parliament gathers for the purpose of persuading the king to spend ever more and more of their money.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: I appreciate what the minister has said, especially his reference to myself, but I fail to see where the saving in interest rates during these last ten years or more has been any remarkable achievement. I should like to ask the minister this question: When he refunds a maturing public debt at a lower rate of interest, is he not just renewing our note at the current rate of interest? Is that not only a business proposition that any of us would carry out?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF MATURED, MATURING AND CALLABLE OBLIGATIONS
speechtext:
Of course it is only a business proposition. However, there is a new aspect to the matter which has arisen in recent years. This country has determined that the control of credit and currency should rest with this parliament, through the government and the Bank of Canada. That fact has an important bearing upon these great refunding operations, in ways which I cannot discuss in this house or indeed on any occasion publicly. However, it is my responsibility. I can assure my hon. friend that there is another important matter to be considered, the choosing of the market, the time and the terms.
Why have I not called these Grand Trunk fours? Perhaps I am wrong, but my judgment is that they should not be called at
C.N.R.-Refunding

the present time and I have so advised my colleagues. Why? Because as a result of long experience in handling these matters I believe that there will be a more advantageous opportunity than the one at present available. We have the right to legislate in regard to the railroads of this country and we are not going to hand the railroads back to anybody at the behest of anybody.
In connection with these perpetual obligations I suggest that if parliament made a mistake and entered into an obligation which in the light of subsequent circumstances, is proving to be ruinous, then there is a duty on subsequent parliaments to change that obligation. That would not be repudiation; it would not be doing anything dishonest; it would be recognizing our high duty to legislate in the best interests of the people.
The suggestion has been made that if we changed the rate of interest we would not save a cent. I submit that if we passed an act appropriating a reduced amount of money, the equivalent of a certain rate of interest, deemed fair, that would not change the essential facts of the situation-or differ from what has been suggested. We can reduce the amount of money payable just the same as we can reduce the rate of interest. That is what has been done in connection with the farmers, as the hon. member for Portage la Prairie has pointed out. The people of western Canada to-day are paying money in freight rates that it was definitely agreed they should not have to pay. The Crowsnest Pass agreement was abrogated by this parliament, and if an obligation to western Canada in regard to freight rates can be abrogated by this parliament, then our obligation to pay money to the bondholders can also be cut down. One is not more sacred than the other.
I cannot sit in my seat in this house, Mr. Chairman, without protesting against the attitude that unless we can get these bondholders to agree to a change we should sit down and do nothing, that if we can not successfully approach them directly we are doing something wrong if we do it indirectly. I submit that if we have a right to legislate to change conditions in regard to freight rates and break a solemn agreement whereby the people of western Canada were promised they would not have to pay more than a certain amount of freight rates on goods shipped into that country; if we can give the

C.N.R.-Refunding
right to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to charge more than that agreed rate, then we can say to the bondholders: After a certain time your bonds are going to be called; if you want your money you can take it, but if you do not, we are going to pay no more than three per cent interest. I submit that there is nothing morally wrong about that, nothing dishonest, and I cannot sit in my seat in this parliament and take the defeatist attitude that unless we can persuade the bondholders to give up the present rate, we can do nothing about it. We sitting here in this parliament of the Dominion of Canada have full legal rights over the matter. When they took these bonds they knew we bad the right to tax them, cancel them-I am not suggesting that we cancel them-do what we saw fit with them. I submit that we shoulS legislate in the light of present day conditions, and fix a rate of interest that will be fair under present conditions.

That at least indicates that the people are quite as well aware of the circumstances as we are in this house, and are quite as anxious as we are to do what can be done. I happened at the moment to be at the finance department, and I was told by the bankers that it was not likely 'that the people would do any such thing; yet the people were so willing to do it that they took $640,000,000 of their high interest securities and converted them to a lower-interest-bearing security. That indicates that the people are interested in the matter and are concerned about it. And they were not the big interests that have been spoken of. You would be amazed, Mr. Chairman, to know that they were people who bought securities in small sums, $5,000, $10,000, some $25,000 and some $100,000, and they took a lower rate of interest because they were willing to help their country at a time of great depression.
I cannot get into my mind how a member of my profession would suggest that when a bargain has been made between two parties by which one of the parties sells his property for a sum of money, and that sum of money is represented by obligations which carry a rate of interest, the other party to the transaction can suddenly say: I am not going to pay what I have agreed to pay you, but I am going to keep the property just 'the same.

workingmen in my province were being paid less than those in other provinces. I considered that to be most unfair. My task was not at all interesting at first and I am thankful to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) for the assistance he provided at that time in helping me to compile and classify these statistics. I also had the help of the staff of the Department of Labour, especially of Mr. Ward, a very competent man who was then deputy minister.
If the hon. member for Kootenay East will look at pages 3654 to 3659 of Hansard of June 12, 1929, he will find a number of tabulations with reference to wages paid in Quebec and other Canadian cities. The minimum and maximum wages paid in Montreal and other Canadian cities are shown. On March 21, 1930, as reported at pages 853 and following of Hansard, the member for Temiscouata made a speech in connection with minimum wages paid to men. He was interrupted by several Tory members. He was interrupted by Mr. Macdougall, who was defeated in Inverness by the present member (Mr. Mac-Lennan); by Mr. Short, who has since died; by Mr. Irvine, who was then a Cooperative Commonwealth Federation member, but who changed his colours quite often; by the Hon. Mr. Chaplin, who has since died, and by Hon. Mr. Geary, the former Minister of Justice. On March 31, 1930, as reported on pages 1132 and following of Hansard, the member for Temiscouata was interrupted again by another Tory who laughed at him when he told about the misery of the unemployed. That was Mr. Ernst, who was afterwards selected as Minister of Fisheries by the then Prime Minister, probably because he was so light. That interruption did not prove a good vote catcher in Nova Scotia.
On April 30, 1930, during the debate on the third reading of the Fair Wages and Hours Act, the member for Temiscouata praised the then Minister of Labour for bringing in that legislation, against which the hon. member voted. I had a complimentary letter from Mr. Tom Moore, then president of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, dated June 18, 1929. I shall not take the trouble to read it, but I keep it on my file. Mr. Moore praised that legislation.
I have in my hand a voluminous report dealing with the settlers on relief in one part of my constituency, which report I can show to anyone who desires to see it. This report concerns a number of men who have suffered considerably. These men come to see me when I am home, and I call to see them

Relief and Agricultural Distress
when. I am in their vicinity. Such visits are a sorrow rather than a pleasure because these men live under such poor circumstances. I have been working for these men; I have been pleading and arguing their case in the house; but what happened? I was made a laughing stock by the Tory gang when I defended these poor settlers who were starving.
Not only that, but I was grossly insulted by a man now employed by the provincial government. At one time he was a member of the press gallery but was expelled because he was a drunkard and a scoundrel. He had space in a room of one of the Tory members where he wrote defamations, calumny and insults in connection with Liberal members, and especially the member for Temiscouata. I called that man by name in the house; but what happened? That man had been evidently inspired, because when I called him a scoundrel, the terrestrial almighty had my words struck from Hansard. This was against all the rules of the house, as we are free to call anyone a scoundrel who is not protected by the rules. I made this statement at that time because I was most indignant, but the hon. gentleman did not defend my action. I was doing my duty in trying to improve the lot of the poor settlers in my constituency and throughout the north, but I was insulted and laughed at by the supporters of the previous government. I am not saying that my hon. friend laughed at me on that occasion ; but he knows those who did, those who jeered at me when I referred to the misery of these men. That may be the reason why he left them. If so, I congratulate him.
Your Honour was in the house at the time and will remember the trouble I had in trying to obtain the previous occupations of the unemployed. I do not know if it is true, but I have been told that an order was then given not to hand out any figures in connection with the unemployed. Figures could be given out only in connection with the employed, but that is an altogether different thing. I could not get any information until the mayors of sixty-two of the most important cities in Canada came to Ottawa. They compiled this information and sent it to me. I had it classified with the help of just one person, and I distributed copies of my report to the members of the house and of the senate. This was declared to be out of
order by the chair as it did not suit the pleasure of the then government. However, I supplied this information in order that the then government and the country should be forced to know something about the previous occupations of the unemployed.
It is utterly impossible to do anything for the rehabilitation of the unemployed unless their previous occupations are known. We must know what they can do and where they can be found. That is why I found the report of the employment commission to be far from satisfactory. The hon. member for Kootenay East has said it is a splendid work, but I consider it a rotten piece of work.

speechtext: I must remind the hon. member that he has exhausted his time.

subsubtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
Go on.
Mr. POULRfT: I offered to do this work, and the only cost to the country would have been the payment of four or five competent employees in the service. Hon. members will remember that was the only condition attached to my offer. If I had done the work, my report probably would have been less extensive; but it would have indicated the previous occupations of each class of unemployed in each important city of Canada, and even in the smaller municipalities, showing what classes of men have suffered from unemployment. That is the only way in which you can draft a sane policy for the rehabilitation of the unemployed. That is my point, Mr. Speaker, and I am not going to continue longer. I thank the committee, and if I have said anything disagreeable it is only because of the respect I have for the truth, my respect for parliament and my respect for my colleagues.

subsubtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) protests very vigorously against the member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) stating that parliament is not doing its duty. I for one want to say that I think parliament is not doing its duty, and that no member of this house can return to his constituency without feeling somewhat ashamed of the small amount of work that 245 men have to show as a result of their deliberations for, now, three sessions.
Referring to the bill now before the house, one cannot estimate its value by itself. That
2350	COMMONS
Relief arid Agricultural Distress
can be done only by examining the policies of the Liberal party as advocated before the election and the policies they have pursued since coming into office.
On February 27, 1933, the leader of the Liberal party set forth in this house the policy of his party with reference to unemployment. Without quoting, one may say that it consisted of four things: (1) Unemployment was to be treated as a national problem; (2) there was to be set up a national employment commission to administer relief in cooperation with the municipalities and in an endeavour to provide work for the unemployed; (3) there was to be set up a system of unemployment insurance; and (4) as a permanent measure the government was going to stimulate internal and external trade.
I ask the house to look very briefly at what has been done and what is now proposed in this bill as an answer to those policies. First of all, may I point out^that the question of unemployment is not being dealt with as a national problem. For the past three sessions we have been told again and again that the direct responsibility lies with the municipalities and the province, and there has been no attempt to come to grips with the problem as the direct responsibility of this parliament and the federal government.
Let us look at the second plank in their platform with reference to unemployment- the setting up of a national employment commission. The idea of a national employment commission was conceived in the mind of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in 1933. It came to birth in 1936, but it was not the kind of child that had been visualized by the Prime Minister. Originally the national employment commission was to be a commission that would cooperate with the provinces in the administration of relief, but the commission that was appointed had no such power, and never has had any such power. It had no power to put a single man to work, no power to administer any relief. As the minister (Mr. Rogers) himself said, it was an advisory commission whose main function was to collect statistics and submit advice to the Minister of Labour.
This commission, conceived in 1933 and bom in 1936, died on February 1, 1938. Shakespeare in Julius Caesar has Mark Antony say, "I come to bury Caesar, not to praise him." This parliament has come to bury the commission, not to praise it. The 
commission is dead; it no longer exists. Having submitted its report, which cost the people of this country in the neighbourhood of $300,000, it now ceases to exist. Why? Is there no longer any need of advice in dealing with the problem of unemployment? Has the problem of unemployment been solved? Even the Minister of Labour would be the first to say that the fact that you have collected statistics regarding unemployment is not removing unemployment, and that an analysis of the situation is not a solution of the problem. Here we have a national employment commission that was to be the bulwark of the Liberal policy for combating unemployment, a commission that was brought into existence in 1936 and died in 1938. But what is most significant of all is that I find, in a return to an order of the house brought down for my colleague the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), that the commission was dismissed before the report which it had submitted had even been considered by the government.

subsubtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: May I correct that? I know my hon. friend wants to be fair. I think he will see that the statement is to the effect that the report was considered, as it only could have been considered, after it had been submitted, and the commission itself was dissolved after it had submitted its final report-its "final report"; I emphasize those words.

subsubtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
The government gave consideration to the final report after its submission, it is true; but the fact still remains that by that time the commission itself had been dismissed, and, strange to say, twelve of the employees whose services with the government had ranged from one to sixteen years, four of them having served for fourteen years and over, were dismissed at the same time. That would look to me, Mr. Speaker, as though there was very little sympathy on the part of the government with the report submitted by the commission. Certainly they have shown no enthusiasm for its recommendations. I ask the house now to look at page 20 of the report of the national employment commission, where will be found a summary of the commission's recommendations. As I intend to speak for only a short time I would ask, with the consent of the house, that this be placed on Hansard.

I ask the house to look at that summary. In. the third column, under the heading, "Action taken," appear the words "Approved July 4, 1936." That was with reference to the registration. Opposite "Employment service" it says:	"No action" "National
Advisory Committee:" "Partially met." "Homeless Adults:" "Approved." "Housing:" "Approved," so far as the first part is concerned, and as to the second part: "No action." "Training and Reconditioning:" "Approved." Then follows a long list opposite which appear the words: "No action," "No action," "No action." "Training centres:" "Partially met." "For the carrying out of training projects:" "Embodied in agreements with provinces."
The thing that impresses me is that, after having paid 8300,000 to secure advice from the best commission the Minister of Labour could get in this country, we find that the term which occurs most often in the third column is, "No action," or "Partially met." I want to suggest that if we are going to bury this commission, we might inscribe on its tombstone the words: "No action," partly as a memorial of its short life, and, second, as a monument to the masterly inaction that has come as a result of its work.
I ask the house to look at some of the things which it did do. Take No. 5 on the statement, "Housing." A great deal has been said in this house about the need of a housing program. But here again we find evidence of what has occurred throughout the government's attempt to meet the problem of unemployment, namely, meeting the shadow of the problem and avoiding the substance. We
have a housing problem and we have a housing scheme, but how much has that scheme benefited the people of Canada? How much has it benefited the people who live in the province from which I come? I find that in Saskatchewan under the dominion housing scheme two houses have been built, at a total expenditure of $8,200. Is it any wonder that the unemployed in Saskatchewan feel that the dominion housing scheme is not an answer to their problem? Certainly two houses will not put many carpenters to work or very much money in the pockets of the merchants and the unemployed.
I turn to another scheme, and one which was a little more successful: The farm placement scheme. Under it there were 42,633 placements and cancellations of 4,752, leaving, I assume, a balance of 37,881. In Saskatchewan, which was the .province which probably most needed it and certainly took the largest advantage of it, there have been 26,858 placements and 4,559 cancellations, leaving 22,299. It is amazing that almost twenty per cent of placements in Saskatchewan under that scheme later had their applications rejected.

subsubtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: What year was that?

subsubtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
This past year. I have before me the answers submitted by the department on that point, relative to the year ended March 14, 1938. When I came to Ottawa last January I was convinced that the whole 4,559 that had been rejected in Saskatchewan were in my constituency, so many people having come to me in connection with this matter; but I have since met

Relief and Agricultural Distress
some hon. gentlemen opposite who seem to be equally convinced that the whole 4,559 were in their constituencies, because so many have been rejected throughout the province.
This was the position, particularly in communities in which there were large families. The father and mother, and one or two members of the family could carry on the farm operations quite easily. They said "Here is an opportunity to put some of our young people out to work"-young people who had been on the relief rolls for several years. They were placed, only to find later that their applications were rejected and they had to come back home. I do not wish to be derogatory of what the minister has tried to do. I appreciate very much the objective he had in mind in the formulation of this scheme. But I think that whoever in his department was responsible for the regulations should be presented with a wooden medal carved out of his own head, because some of these regulations are nothing but sheer nonsense.
I have examined the rejections-there is quite a large number of them-which have come to my hand, and they fall roughly into four classes: First of all, those who were rejected because they were not homeless; that is, their parents resided within a radius of twelve or fifteen miles. Of course that is absurd. These young people had to be placed where they could find some farmer who would take them. The fact that their parents lived twelve miles or a hundred and twelve miles away made little or no difference as to whether or not they were carrying on the work that was intended under the scheme. Others, strange to say, were rejected because they had never been employed and therefore could not be considered employable. We in Saskatchewan have had very severe conditions since 1931. Many of these people left school in that year and have been unemployed more or less ever since. How long does a young man or a young woman have to be unemployed before he or she is considered employable? If conditions like this continue, you will find young men beginning to grow a beard and yet able to say that they were never employed and are therefore unemployable.

subsubtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: How many fall into that category.

subsubtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
Of course 1 could not give the minister any statistical information, but I would say a large number who have come to my attention are in that classification. Others were rejected because, it was said, there was not enough work on the farm. I should like to see, and I am sure

the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) would also like to see, a farm where there is not enough work for a hired man at a time when there is stock to look after, chores to do, machinery to get ready and, in cases where they have it, seed to clean during the winter. But these people were rejected because, it was said, there was not enough work to warrant the hiring of a man.
One other classification refers to relatives. I have mentioned to the minister during this session the case of a young man whose sister lost her husband and was left with a small family on the farm. This young man left his job and took over his sister's farm, managed it; but that year he had no crop; he made application to the Saskatchewan government, was accepted, and for two years was under the farm placement scheme, the authorities knowing perfectly well that he was a relative of the employer. Last year he was cut off. He has loyally stayed with his sister and helped her manage the farm and look after her small family, but is not paid, as are other boys in the community doing less work than he does. Mr. Molloy, who is administering the act in Saskatchewan, and Mr. Parker, the minister of municipal affairs, said that there were a number of such cases and that they had made strong representations to the Minister of Labour and the federal government asking them to change that regulation in the direction of making it more elastic, but they could get no response. I suggest that the men in the several provinces who are administering the act are in a much better position to set these regulations than is someone in Ottawa who is not actually in contact with the problem.
I come now to another matter which is dealt with under this bill, namely agricultural aid, or as the bill says, " alleviation of agricultural distress." Of course the tragedy is that after three years of a bill like this agricultural distress is still present in some parts of the west in an even more acute form than before. I left my constituency last Saturday after visiting farms on which there was not a single kernel of feed or seed; the farmers had lost half of the horses.-and they were not old horses-which they sent to the Carberry pasture. One man who had weighed two horses which he sent to Manitoba found that they had each lost in the neighbourhood of five hundred pounds. Farmers with moisture conditions such as they have not had for years, and with a good price, are facing the spring almost destitute, with no feed for their horses with which to get their land into shape and, prior to last Saturday at any rate, no

Relief and Agricultural Distress
seed at hand. One of the amusing things is the attitude of some of the men who are responsible for administering this system. I wrote to the manager of the grain and fodder branch of the Saskatchewan government, after having taken up the matter with the federal Minister of Agriculture, with reference particularly to chicken feed, and I received a letter in which this striking paragraph occurs:
We are of the opinion that the majority of farmers should secure sufficient feed from the screenings of their seed grain to take care of their poultry feed requirements.
They are to take the screenings from their seed grain to feed their poultry; but if they have not any seed, what are they to do? One can take screenings from seed; but if there is no seed, where are the screenings to come from? That is the situation with regard to agricultural aid, a condition which is sad in the extreme. People are depending upon the government for seed which is not there, and when it gets there the benefit will not be what we have been led to believe, because we are told that repairs will have to be deducted and that the seed will have to be cleaned, this being another deduction of ten or fifteen per cent from the total amount. The result is that the farmers will face the summer with weakened horses, poor stock, and very little seed with which to seed their land.
I come now to the third plank in the Liberal policy with reference to unemployment, and that was the setting up of a national system of unemployment insurance. In this regard there is only one question that I would ask: Where is this promised system of. unemployment insurance? This is the third session of parliament and we have not yet seen this national system of unemployment insurance. True, we shall be told that some of the provinces would not agree. But that was not what was said in 1933 in this house; that was not what was said in 1935 on the hustings. We were not told then that the provinces would have to agree. In fact, on the night of the election the present Prime Minister in his speech to the people of Canada over the radio said:
The whole-hearted cooperation of the Liberal premiers and governments of eight of the nine provinces of Canada was an exceptionally significant feature of the campaign and one which may be expected to contribute in no uncertain way to the solution of many of our country's perplexing problems.
We were led to understand then that with Liberal governments in a majority of the provinces and with a Liberal government here at Ottawa, there would be no difficulty in giving the people of Canada what had
been promised, namely, a national system of unemployment insurance. But where is that national system of unemployment insurance?
I have here a piece of campaign literature published by the Edmonton East federal Liberal association, entitled: "Let us get going again." There is a picture of the Liberal candidate. Beneath, it says: "Read the Liberal government's record of promises and fulfilment." On one side there appear the promises and on the other side is the fulfilment. I will not read them all; but this is No. 9, unemployment insurance. That is the promise. Here is the fulfilment:
A national system of unemployment insurance has been introduced .	. . but the Alberta
Social Credit government has refused to cooperate.
A national system has been introduced! Where is it? Well, I have read through the order paper with a normal amount of intelligence, and I cannot find in it any bill providing for a national system of unemployment insurance; yet here are the people of Edmonton East being told in a by-election, in a pamphlet officially issued by the Liberal party, that the system has been introduced. We have heard a great deal this session about making politics clean, taking bribery out of it, and so on, but I want to know how you will take this kind of thing out. People were actually led to believe during the recent byelection that a national system of unemployment insurance had been introduced, when no such thing has been done at all. And judging by the indications, it does not look as if it is going to be introduced. Of course, the Minister of Agriculture, who commanded the government forces on the field of battle there, may be able to give some explanation; but certainly I cannot find any in the legislation which the government has submitted this session.
The fourth plank of the Liberal party's platform with regard to unemployment, and the one which the Minister of Labour emphasized the other day, was that as a permanent measure to solve the unemployment situation they were pinning their faith to the stimulation of internal and external trade. While there is a measure of truth in that, this is also true, that any country which to-day pins its faith to external trade as a means of solving the unemployment situation is leaning on an extremely fluctuating factor. You have only to look back over the export trade of Canada in the last six months to see how unstable a factor it is.

subsubtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
Surely it is a very necessary condition.

Relief and Agricultural Distress

subsubtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Yes, but the hon. member did not tell his constituents in 1935 that that was the only condition.

subsubtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: No one has suggested that in this house.

subsubtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: I have outlined four things and none of the first three have been fulfilled. The only promise that has been partly fulfilled is the last one, the expansion of external trade, and that is a fluctuating factor which has been decreasing in the last few months rather than increasing. But even an expansion of external trade will not meet the problem of technological displacement which is constantly going on in industry. I have in mind several men of my own acquaintance who used to earn on railway pumps between $125 and $150 a month. They had been working for from fifteen to twenty years for the railways, but the automatic pumps came in and they have been unemployed since 1931. They spent the best years of their life at that work. You cannot make them motor mechanics or radio builders or aviators.

subsubtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: If a man has been working for twenty years, getting from $150 to $180 a month, has there not been some obligation on him to provide for a period such as this?

subsubtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: To begin with, I said $125 to $150. But is the hon. gentleman suggesting that any man who has been working for fifteen or twenty years for $125 a month could have saved money out of that to keep him the rest of his days and to take care of his family?

subsubtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Many have done it.

subsubtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
I am sure the hon. gentleman is not suggesting that has constituents should all try to do it. The fact is that in consequence of new machinery, men are being displaced to-day and labour is not sufficiently mobile to allow them to be transferred suddenly from the industry in which they were engaged to the production of the new machines that are displacing labour. You have therefore a class of labour that cannot be absorbed through the normal expansion of trade, and nothing to date has been suggested or done by this government to meet that situation.
The cry is constantly made that certain groups in this house criticize but offer no suggestion. Without going into the matter in detail, I want to remind the government that suggestions have come constantly from this comer for three consecutive sessions. For instance, we suggested a building program, a program for the removal of slums, not only urban but rural slums. I have had the

privilege at different times of visiting most of the larger cities of the United Kingdom and the United States and some of the cities of Europe. I assisted at one time in drawing up a research survey regarding the lamentable housing conditions in one of the largest cities of the United States. But I have seen housing conditions in western Canada, let alone eastern Canada, that almost beggar description. We have in Saskatchewan the unenviable distinction of having the smallest number pro rata of houses with sanitary conveniences in all Canada. In northeastern Saskatchewan, in the town of Crooked River, where they have a huge lumber mill turning out millions of feet of lumber a year, within 300 yards of where the lumber is produced there are the worst shacks I have ever seen.
We have suggested not only the clearance of slums but the building of low rental homes. We have suggested the need for building schools and hospitals. One has only to see the country schools, with cracked plaster, insufficient warmth for cold days, broken seats, dilapidated floors, to realize that people could be put to work all across Canada in the erection, not of useless buildings, or buildings that are almost never used, such as some armouries, but schools, hospitals, libraries and decent homes. Roads need to be built. The other day I came across a statement in the Liberal paper in Regina, the Leader-Post. It is not often I agree with what it says, but I am in hearty agreement with this. It is headed:
A Tragedy
Can anyone doubt the point that it would be better to spend even more money and get something in return rather, than spend what is being spent to-day without anything being done except to proclaim to the world that thousands of people are living on direct relief and must take their living without working? The millions of dollars that have been spent to keep people in idleness will remain one of the tragedies of the non-production period in western Canada. It is not too late to make a start.
I recommend that to the Minister of Labour. It is not too late even yet, half-way through the teirm of this parliament as we are, to make a start to put people to work, to pay them wages which will enable them to buy goods at the stores and send some orders to the warehouses and factories. We have suggested pensions to take care of the aged and those physically incapable of supporting themselves and their families.

subsubtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to make a few observations respecting Bill No. 105, a measure to assist in the alleviation of unemployment and agricultural distress, introduced by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers). I trust it is wide enough to permit the government to do that which, in its own judgment, it believes should be done to handle the present situation.
From the experience I have had I am going to make some suggestions to-night which I would hope, if put into effect, so far as my own



Relief and Agricultural Distress
section of the country is concerned, would be exceedingly beneficial and would prevent handouts and bonuses. From my acquaintance with the people of my constituency I know that they want work, not doles. The lumber business, with which I was connected for many years, coupled with the pulp and paper business, gives more employment than any other single industry in Canada. I believe, if there could be some stimulation given to lumbering, and at the same time if there were a possibility of accomplishing that which I shall suggest, we would go a great way towards relieving unemployment in my section of Canada.
For several years the Dominion Housing Act has been on the statute books of Canada and, so far as it has gone, has worked splendidly. But in order to avail oneself of the privileges extended under the housing act one must have twenty per cent of the amount to be borrowed; otherwise he cannot come under the act. In that way a great proportion of the population is eliminated. There is the further criticism that in many communities almost two years elapsed before the act became effective. That condition arose because the trust companies were not keen on availing themselves of the privileges of the legislation. They realized that when they accepted the government's proposal under the Dominion Housing Act, it would mean that their interest rates on other loans would have to be reduced. Even during the depression years between 1930 and 1935 those companies still thought that interest rates of seven per cent or six and a half per cent were not too high. Therefore some time elapsed before the act came into real operation.
Otherwise it has worked well, and is possibly doing what the government had in mind when the act was passed. Now, when a good loan comes along, the trust companies take it up entirely, and it does not come under the housing act. It would seem, therefore, that the measure has only had the effect of persuading the trust companies to make more loans for housing purposes.
The other measure passed by this government was the home improvement plan. Certainly the home improvement plan has given a considerable amount of work, has stimulated business in communities and, much more important, in some measure has encouraged the banks to make individual loans. Certainly that is beneficial to the community.
But a great part of the population did not derive the benefits of either of these pieces of legislation. If you can stimulate the lumber

business; if you can create homes for working men, without cost to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) or to the country, and if you can make those loans self-liquidating, the government receiving interest on its money, you will have a worth-while project.
I am suggesting to-night that, under Bill No. 105 now before the house, a workman's housing scheme should be inaugurated, the details of which I shall outline.
Much of what I shall say will be confined to observations respecting conditions in my home town. Between the years 1930 and 1937, a period when we experienced the greatest depression through which we have ever gone, besides paying its way the city of Sherbrooke reduced its capital debt by $654,700. Therefore that city is in a financial position which would make it possible to cooperate under the scheme I shall suggest. A further matter to which I direct the attention of the house is that in 1937, out of a population of 32,500 people, six thousand hands were employed in twenty-eight of Sherbrooke's industries. One company which in 1934 employed 438 hands now employs 1,200; another formerly employing 570 now employs 650; another formerly employing 370 now employs 725; another formerly employing 433 now employs 500, and another formerly employing 971 now employs 1,150. I give these figures, not to boast, but to prove that a great proportion of the people of Sherbrooke are in the category of working men.
I am suggesting that we inaugurate a workingmen's housing scheme, so that people such as I have mentioned, earning from $18 to $30 a week, can build homes of their own and be enabled over a number of years to become the proprietors of those homes. Someone may say that at those wages such a scheme is impossible. May I point out that a company with which I was connected before 1929 built fifty homes, without any cash payments, and sold them to fifty home owners. The records show the results of those loans. In passing, may I state that the scheme was carried out with money drawing seven per cent interest. The principal sums were paid in monthly payments extending over eighteen and a half years. There were only seven losses on the fifty homes, and some of those losses were only partial. I shall not take time to give the reasons for the losses, but I am satisfied that in a future scheme they could be eliminated.
First, we must agree on the principle that the working man with the desire to own his own home can pay for it only on the condition that the payment does not exceed one week's wages in each month. If a man is

Relief and Agricultural Distress
drawing $18 a week during the year, he is able to pay up to $18 a month towards owning his own home. In other words, so long as the payments for home ownership do not exceed twenty-five per cent-they are better at twenty per cent-the scheme is perfectly feasible, without loss.

Eighteen mills. Three and a half per cent of $2,600 is $91. A payment of $50 on the capital would bring this to $141. The tax at eighteen mills, eleven mills for municipal purposes and seven mills for schools, would be $36 on a $2,000 valuation. This would make a total payment of $177 for the first year, which would mean a monthly payment of $14.75 to cover interest, capital and taxes.
The mayor of the city suggested the other day that if a housing scheme could be put into effect to give employment to plumbers, roofers and carpenters, to take up the unemployment in Sherbrooke practically one hundred per cent, they would give a five year exemption from taxes on all workingmen's homes constructed under the scheme. I doubt whether they have the right to do that, but the chairman of the finance committee told me that in any case there would be a three year exemption from taxes. However, I would not consider this in the scheme. If the city was not to impose taxes for three or five years, I would suggest that the taxes be included in the monthly payments and a reserve fund created against future payments until such time as taxes were charged.
Without going into detail, if the house cost $2,500 and the lot $300, the monthly payment would amount to $15.33. On a $3,000 maximum cost house, the monthly payment would be $16. This would include interest on the money borrowed, taxes, supervision by the city and payments on the principal in order to make the loan self-liquidating.
Mr. ST. PERE: That is on houses of wooden construction.

speechtext:
Of wooden construction. This would stimulate the lumber industry and create employment in the woods and sawmills of the country. Employment would be given to tradesmen of all kinds in the cities, and the local store trade in nails, cement, roofing and commodities of that nature would be stimulated.
This scheme could be put through without costing the country a single cent. It would be a great improvement over handing out money to people who can find nothing else to do but stay at home. The people in my constituency do not want doles; all they want is a chance to work. I hope the government will put such a scheme into operation so that homes may be provided for our workingmen. I shall not go into the other side of the picture; but we all know what it would mean to Sherbrooke, to the townships and to all of Canada, when our working people have equities in their homes. After a man has made his payments for five years and his wife has fixed up the grounds by planting flowers and so on; after he becomes a proprietor instead of a rentee, the whole future is changed. You have a different condition existing when people have a stake in the country instead of being at the mercy of employers.
I have another more serious suggestion to make. In my opinion we should immediate.1''' take up the question of slum clearance. In all the cities of Canada-and Sherbrooke-is no exception-we find fine paved streets and all the necessary accommodations for comfortable living. More and more as the years go by we find our cities cleaner and more beautiful. But in every one of these municipalities we find a certain proportion of homes, not only below standard but some not as good as the place where some people keep their horses. They are unfit for human habitation. We intend to spend money to create employment, so we should start immediately to do away with some of these unsatisfactory conditions in our cities.
These slum areas are not large. In the city of Sherbrooke there are possibly no more than one hundred homes unfit for
^360

Relief and Agricultural Distress
human habitation. Someone will say immediately, "Oh, well, you have a statute; you can condemn these homes." I would reply that if a family is renting such a place from the owner at a low rent and you condemn the property, you will have quite a proposition on your hands. What I would suggest is that the property be condemned as unfit for human habitation. Then the owner should be supplied with a plan of reconstruction and the place either burned down or torn down. Of course, before that is done the family would be taken out. Then a new home would be built according to government plan and, when completed, the previous tenants would be moved in. The owner would be subsidized to the extent of say fifty per cent of the difference between the municipal valuation and the cost of the new construction. Before the new house was commenced, .a contract would be made with the owner to provide that the rent would not be increased for the same family for from two to five years.
There is another side to this situation. It so happens that in these one hundred homes there is a greater population of children per home than in any other section of Sherbrooke. If children are to be allowed to grow up under these conditions, our future generations will have to pay. If the situation is corrected immediately, we shall be creating a future asset. I do not advocate this because I want to spend money; I do it because I want every citizen to have a chance. I feel our workmen have a right to a chance to own their own homes. The farmer has the right to rebuild his home at decent rates of interest. We could stimulate employment throughout the length and breadth of this country and, I believe, eliminate the dole system one hundred per cent.
There is one other side to this slum clearance question. Some will say that this is paternalism, but I know whereof I speak when I say what I am going to say. In each of these communities there should be appointed, in addition to the health officer, a fully *qualified woman to supervise these new homes and the families living therein. The homes should be inspected for cleanliness and a watch kept over the progress the family is making. This woman would be the contact point between the family and the community. If this were done, within a few years time we would see a difference in the younger generation in our country.
I have one thing more to say and then I have finished. In every one of our cities there is a shortage of playgrounds and parks.

If there is one class of work which with others could be done under this legislation to advantage, it is the improvement of city parks, national parks, and the playgrounds of Canada. The longer the hours our people work who are employed in the cotton and silk industries, and the textile industries generally, as well as other classes of industries, and the more members of the family employed in them, the greater is the need for open spaces throughout the community for recreation. So, Mr. Speaker, I leave with you the consideration of these suggestions. One plan is one hundred per cent self-liquidating; the other will not cost this country very much money; it is in any case one which will provide work, instead of the dole, and it is a work that could well be done under this Bill No. 105 of the Minister of Labour.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have no desire to attempt to embarrass the government in any way or to hinder the progress of this bill. I realize that at the present time it is either this bill or nothing, but if I am in order I should like to make a few general remarks on the subject of unemployment.
Unemployment is a comparatively new thing in Canada, but it is an old story in Great Britain. It dates in its present form from the industrial revolution and the development of what is known as orthodox economics. It is not too much to say that the original orthodox economists regarded unemployment as not only inevitable but as a necessity because the industrial revolution was based on cheap production; cheap production means cheap wages, and the surest way to keep wages down is to take away all *protection from the worker so that he must either work or starve. The economist Ricardo, in his Iron Law of Wages, said that the wages of the labourers must be such that one with the other they could reproduce their numbers without increase or decrease, and he thought the probability was that they would be less rather than more; but when their sufferings and privations had so reduced their numbers, then by that very decrease their wages would rise to the subsistence level. Not only was that doctrine accepted by the economists, but it was accepted by the church, by religion itself. Malthus wrote many books *on the subject, and he was fully of the opinion, as were the majority of religious people of those days, that the only possible use for the labouring classes was labour, and that if they produced more children than there was a market for, the proper method of dealing with the problem was to starve them to death. That is literally true, and

Relief and Agricultural Distress
any suggestions that those conditions could be improved for the victims of the system were met with ridicule or contempt.
A hundred years ago in Great Britain children six and seven years of age were worked fifteen hours a day, mainly to reduce the wages of their parents, and when people objected that it could not be right to work children in that manner they were told that Satan finds mischief for idle hands to do, very much as we hear to-day.
Roughly one hundred years ago the then government in Great Britain was faced with a very nice problem of deciding the standard of relief. If they put the standard of relief any lower than the standard of wages, then the recipients of relief would have starved to death. But if not lower, then the workers would say: Why should we work when those on relief are getting as much as we are. So the government of that day set their economists to work to find ways and means of administering relief in the most objectionable and degrading way. Any amelioration of the condition of the poor of Great Britain was due, not to the economists or to the church, but to the efforts of a few men who refused to believe that any such practice was necessary to keep any system going, and that if it was necessary, then the system itself should be done away with.
I have heard many members say that what the people want is work. I should like to say that from my observations in the country, what the people want is security, and that is not quite the same as work. What they want is worth-while work and worth-while wages, and not work for work's sake.
I am perfectly in agreement with any scheme of house-building. In fact, there is no reason in the world, since we have the labour, the materials, the machinery and the knowledge, why we could not rebuild Canada from one end to the other. There is no real reason why we could not do it, although I know that according to the canons of sound finance it cannot be done because we cannot find the money. I think the experience of Great Britain over the last one hundred and fifty years is proof enough that there is no solution for the problem of unemployment under orthodox economics and sound money. In fact, the one is the outcome of the other. There are palliatives such as the dole, and so on, but there is no cure for unemployment under the existing system.
There are a great many contradictions which I have heard mentioned in this house and which, of course, one finds in all books dealing with orthodox economics.
Let me emphasize that the object of industry is not work and wages; its only objects are goods and services. Anybody who ever had1 a job of production to do knows that he must produce the greatest possible amount of goods with the least possible amount of labour. Under the competitive system, if one is to survive it is necessary to cut labour-costs. When we do that we reduce purchasing power, so that those who produce the goods are unable to consume them ; hence the drive for foreign trade and foreign markets. That is one contradiction.
Then I find contempt extending even to-recipients of old age pensions. I cannot see why it is that a man who has worked faithfully and steadily for a lifetime should be-regarded, when he becomes too old to work,, as an object of charity. On the other hand, people who have never done a useful day's work in their lives, and never intend to, but happen to be the fortunate recipients of private money, are regarded with every mark of respect. At the same time any suggestion to distribute purchasing power to the people in general seems to be regarded as a threat to the morals of the country; it is said that we want to demoralize the people. Yet the object of any person who provides his family with insurance is that his family, so far as he can make it possible, shall be granted economic security, so that they cannot be put to work but they can put themselves to work, which is a very different thing.
I might mention the quintuplets, who are regarded as the most valuable children in Ontario and perhaps in Canada, and are the objects of the provincial government's greatest and most careful regard. Everything has been done to safeguard the welfare of those famous children. Already, at their tender age, they have been provided, I understand, with a fund of 8100,000 apiece. If that is good for the "quints", because $100,000 means economic freedom; if that is the best and the finest thing which the government can do for those five children, why is it the finest thing for poor children that they shall be-destitute and forced to work under any conditions?
I have spoken of work for work's sake. Last summer there was a road rebuilt in Alberta^ from Edmonton south. In order to employ' as many people as possible they scrapped a lot of machinery and put numbers of men to>
work with picks and shovels. They made a splendid road; but when the taxpayers saw the bill there was such a fuss made that the government was forced to appoint a royal commission to inquire into the cost

Relief and Agricultural Distress
of construction, because, instead of using machinery-and that is what machinery is for-they put as many men to work as possible.
We are very fond of praising thrift. Thrift is regarded as one of the greatest of virtues. People are told to save; that is, to consume less; at the same time they are told to work harder, which, of course, means to produce more. How can the same lot of people continue to produce more and to consume less?
Finally, while the government and other agencies are putting men to work, science is putting them out of work as fast as it can. The whole thing is a contradiction.
In 1931, during the time that Ramsay MacDonald was Prime Minister of Great Britain, that country was threatened with being driven off gold. In order to preserve the gold standard, Mr. MacDonald and his government approached the hankers of Paris and ILondon for the purpose of borrowing gold. One of the main conditions of the loan was that the social services of Great Britain should be reduced, the dole be cut and the administration of it made as nauseous as possible. All social services were diminished. What was the consequence? For one thing, a mutiny of the fleet occurred, and there was such an outcry that the government was forced from office and the country driven off gold. And when the gold standard was done away with, better times and more employment followed immediately.
As I said before, what the people want is security; and as they are British people, with that security they desire freedom. But if they are driven far enough they will forego even their freedom in order to get security. That has happened in Germany and Italy, and it will happen here if we continue the way we are going.
As I see the matter, there are only two solutions. The one is enforced labour-put the people to work. That means fascism; it provides security, but also it involves loss of liberty. The other is, so to alter and adapt <our financial system that anything physically posable and desirable becomes financially possible, to the end that the people of this ^country can consume to the limits of their desires or of their powers to produce. In that way the people will not only gain security but will retain their liberty.

speechtext:
If this hon. house will bear with me for a few moments, I shall endeavour to submit a few observations on one of the suggested cures for unemployment. It is
[Mr. Jaques.l
difficult, of course, to find an absolute corrective to do away with this scourge in just a single operation. It would be so nice to launch an attack on the entire front and keep it up until the enemy had been driven out of the country. But it is evident that only the combination of the best means, where each can achieve the best results, will bring about the desired success.
It is not necessary to point out to hon. members that one of the worst causes of the depression is due to the desertion of the land. Steps must be taken first to stop this desertion and then to go on with colonization.
The national employment commission gives, on page 8 and following of its report, a list of practical measures to increase employment, and in that list, at page 12, it recommends rehabilitation through land settlement. In my opinion we have there a proposal that deserves the best consideration of the house and of the country, a proposal that should be thoroughly explored because it harbours great possibilities of permanent relief for a considerable number of people. No one will object to my statement that Canada was a good deal more prosperous when there was a better balance between the proportions of urban and rural population. Let us see just what has been the trend of population in Canada. I have here figures taken from the Canada Year Book, French edition, for 1937, the figures covering the last five census periods. In 1891, the total rural population was 3,296,141 and the urban population only 1,537,- 098, or about half. In 1901, the rural population had increased to 3,357,000 and the urban population had gone up to 2,000,000 in round figures. In 1911, there was a further increase in rural population but not quite so large as in the urban population, because the figures for 1911 show that the rural population in that year was nearly 4,000,000, or, to be exact, 3,933,696, whereas the urban population had gone up to 3,272,947. In 1921, conditions were still more serious because the rural population had risen to 4,435,000 and the urban population was 4,352,000. In other words, they were just about equal. The last census in 1931 showed that the rural population was 4,800,000, while the cities had risen to 5,572,000.
If hon. members will look at the increase by provinces they will find the same thing proportionately. For the information of members from the province of Quebec I shall give the figures for our province.
