These figures reveal an evil situation. They are appalling and should impress everyone with the absolute necessity of stopping the desertion of the soil. In my humble opinion there should be no delay in arranging a plan of colonization more vigorous than heretofore. I do not think much can be expected in getting settlers from the cities. It is difficult to convince men and women who go to the cities from the rural districts of the advisability of returning to the land. My suggestion is that farmers' sons shoidd be encouraged to take up land for themselves, because they would be better qualified than any other portion of the population. They have the necessary training and would succeed more easily than people sent to the rural districts from the cities, sometimes at great expense. It so happens also that in the farming districts a large number of farmers have large families, and of course one farm can be passed on only to one son. If the farmer has four or five other sons, they too should be helped to get farms; otherwise they drift to the cities and increase unemployment. They should be given every chance, and no doubt the national employment commission had that in mind, because on page 13 they make the following suggestion:
_ Assistance to be given in three ways, namely in the form of:-
(a)	Roads, bridges, schools, guidance and advice in their work, to be a free gift to the communities of settlers and not repayable.
(b)	Bonuses for clearing land, and bringing it under cultivation, not to be repayable but to vary inversely with the value of the timber removed.
I submit that this matter should be gone into thoroughly and some arrangement made with the provincial governments to carry out a plan of this sort, because I am sure that in the extension of such a program we shall find a safe way of providing permanent relief for a considerable number of people.

subsubtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
I wonder if the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Howard) would mind if, before I begin my remarks in connection with this bill, I were to congratulate him upon the excellent and constructive speech he delivered earlier this evening. I hope the government will take note of it, because there are many suggestions in it that are worth while, suggestions that would help, not only to overcome unemployment, but also, as he has pointed out, to make this world a better place to live in.
The Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers), when moving the second reading of the bill, said that it was similar to the one passed last year. That, in my opinion, is one of the most serious objections to the bill. I have been in this house since 1930, and we have had a bill similar to this one in every session beginning with 1931. This is the eighth bill that has been introduced here to do what this bill is supposed to do-to deal with unemployment relief in its various aspects. I admit that in the earlier days of the depression there was some reason for the belief that unemployment as we then had it and as it now exists was really a temporary matter, and that the bills introduced for the first few years were to meet a temporary emergency. There was some valid reason for that, although I believe a close analysis would indicate that it was only what we could expect. But I submit that after eight years of such conditions as we have had, we ought to have something of a more permanent nature to deal with unemployment and the effects of unemployment than has as yet been placed before us. And particularly have we a right to expect something more from this government. I have, as I said, been in-this house since 1930, and I remember very well that the matter for which the former government was criticized the most was the temporary nature of their measures for dealing with unemployment. To-day there is no valid reason for considering the situation brought about by the depression of 1929 as something requiring only temporary remedies. As long as our present system continues, there is every reason to consider the depression as a permanent condition.
I have been surprised, as I am sure other hon. members have, at the poverty of legislation on the order paper during this session, when so many pressing problems are facing the country. I am sure that the people throughout the dominion are becoming alarmed at the lack of any measure for dealing with their problems. A few days after I [DOT]arrived in Ottawa to attend the session a newspaperman came into my office and asked about the news from the west. In the course

Relief and Agricultural Distress
of our conversation lie made this statement, the truth of which has become more and more apparent to me as the session continues. He said, "You cannot get news or anything that *makes copy these days in Ottawa. When Bennett was in office he was always doing something; you might not like what he was doing but he was doing something. This government does not do anything but sit and think. Come to think of it," he said, "they do not even think; they just sit." As I have sat here day after day since the beginning of the session and watched the order paper and its poverty of constructive legislation, I am more and more convinced of the truth of what my newspaper friend said. The government act as if nothing of a serious nature confronted us. They seem to have a sort of childlike faith that things will right themselves, if they only wait long enough; that trade conditions will improve. That is the most childish idea of all. It indicates that they believe trade is the cause of economic activity. Trade is not the cause; it is the effect of economic activity. This government, as I have pointed out on one or two occasions during the past couple of years, were fortunate in coming into office at a time when trade all over the world was increasing, and they were not slow to take credit to themselves for that increase. But to-day trade is declining. During the last six months there has been a significant decline in the trade of Canada, especially our export trade. Does the government accept responsibility for the decline? There came to me from the bureau of statistics recently a compilation of figures showing the trade of Canada by months for the last fiscal year ended March 31. I noticed in that return that there has been a substantial decline in our export trade for six consecutive months from October, 1937. In that period the aggregate decline as compared with the same six months of last year was over $82,000,000. That means an average decline of over $13,000,000 each month for the last six months.

subsubtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Does the hon. member think the drought had anything to do with that?

subsubtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
I have no doubt it had something to do with it. But if we should happen to have a bumper crop in western Canada this year and they also have bumper crops in other parts of the world, prices will be so low that there will be a further decrease in our trade figures. That would not be due to the drought, it would be due to too much production. So it does not do to put too many of our burdens on the Lord, because He is not altogether responsible.

The total decline in trade has been substantial, and there is no assurance whatever that that decline will not continue. To support that contention I will quote briefly from the monthly letter of the Canadian Bank of Commerce for April, 1938. Reviewing general conditions in Canada, the letter says on page 3:
Indeed, the seasonal gains have this year been so small and confined to such a narrow field that business activity as a whole is now about fifteen per cent below that of the early spring of 1937. A lesser rate of decline would of course be evident were it not for the new fears and uncertainties arising from the European political situation which have spread to this country, as they have to every other part of the world .	.	.
It has now become clearly apparent that the hopes of maintaining business activity at its present level are pinned on domestic agricultural conditions, especially those in the western grain belt, for it is unlikely that any other important stimuli can be felt before the late summer or early autumn.
As I said before, even if conditions are good in the western grain fields this autumn, we can expect no improvement unless conditions are bad in the grain fields in some other parts of the world.
I would have waited until this bill had gone into committee before making any extended remarks on it, were it not for the fact that the situation in my own city is causing the authorities there grave concern. They have made their difficulties known to the federal government and also to the provincial government. They are greatly alarmed as to what may happen in Vancouver, because of the number of single men without employment now congregated in that city. The unemployment figures for March 1 of this year in Vancouver show that there were 6,878 cases on relief. That is about a thousand less than there were last year. These are heads of families, single unemployed men and unemployed women who are on relief, and the dependants of families are not included. When the dependants are included, the number on relief amounts to 21,094. This, again, is lower than it was a year ago. But a year ago we were beginning a very rapid economic improvement, and this year the tendencies are all the other way.
To-day there are in Vancouver about 5,000 single unemployed men who were working on forestry projects during the winter months. I am told these men will have a small amount of back pay to keep them going for a week or two. But about the first or second week of May that back pay will be used up, and so far no provision has been made for these men. The city feels that it is not in a

Relief and Agricultural Distress
financial position to cany them. Unless something is done quickly, trouble will ensue.
I have before me a copy of a letter I received from the acting mayor. In it is quoted a telegram sent to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers). A telegram was forwarded to me about the same time, but when I asked a question of the minister in the house I was not given an opportunity to read that telegram. Writing to me on March 24 in connection with the telegram to the Minister of Labour, the acting mayor said:
On the 23rd instant, after a long discussion by the council on relief matters, the following telegram was dispatched to the Hon. Mr. Norman Rogers, Minister of Labour:
"The relief problem as submitted to the Vancouver city council by the provincial government (particularly with respect to the single unemployed), is beyond our financial power to carry out, and your government's help is urgently needed, if serious trouble is to be avoided."
Amplifying the telegram the acting mayor goes on to say:
The resolution which authorized it directed that letters be sent by air mail to the Vancouver members at Ottawa apprising them of the desperate situation which has made necessary the sending of the above telegram. The seasonal relief problem confronting Vancouver, which during the last several years has been serious due to the large number of transient single men, has been aggravated to unprecedented proportions this year by the enforcement of the terms of the new federal-provincial relief agreement. The effect of this agreement is that the provincial government, facing reduced grants in aid from federal sources, has passed participation in the financial responsibility in several new categories to the city of Vancouver. The extent of this financial burden has not yet been determined, but it has been estimated to range from between $25,000 to $30,000 a month. For several years the city, as you are aware, has been pressed to the extreme to meet its proportion of the relief load which has been carried, and now comes the addition of the categories mentioned above. . . .
Two courses of action are open to the city. That is, the further reduction of necessary public services already seriously curtailed, or the refusal to grant assistance in any form to large numbers of destitute persons which will, of course, lead to serious disorders with accompanying loss of property and possibly life. Might I reiterate to you that we are not overemphasizing the extreme seriousness of the problem as faced by the city to-day, and its utter financial inability to meet it from its own resources.
This is a situation which has periodically faced Vancouver during the last five or six years. In 1933, 1934 and 1935 men were taken to the camps, and then would either be released from them or simply leave them and come to the city. While in theory the
camps have been abolished and the men put to work on other projects, when those projects are completed or closed down temporarily the men come back to the city, and the problem is renewed.
Now the city fears that the care of these men will become a permanent charge, and one which it is absolutely unable to carry. On March 8 of this year the union of British Columbia municipalities laid their case before the provincial cabinet, and I should like to read briefly from their presentation. They said:
When the provincial government passed to the local areas, through the medium of the municipal act, the burden of caring for their destitute and indigent it was transferring a duty imposed upon it by the federal government, through the British North America Act. In pre-depression days this burden was only nominal but, as a result of the eight-year period of relief, the entire problem has been changed. Contributing factors are:
I should like the Minister of Labour and other members of the government to take notice of the contributing factors in British Columbia:
(1) The influx into British Columbia municipalities of large numbers of transient families and individuals, whose previous domicile was outside of the province. Many of these whose almost entire residence in British Columbia has been established while in receipt of public assistance, are now municipal responsibilities, under the Residence and Responsibility Act.
Particularly in the case of single men, during the period of federal administration of relief camps, assistance was granted without reference to residence. British Columbia, with its more attractive climate, drew large numbers of handicapped or near unemployable types who, being unfit for camp, were maintained in municipal areas, and who will now be left in the wake of unemployment relief, as a municipal heritage.
The brief of the union of municipalities goes on to deal with other matters, but I shall take time to quote only one further paragraph:
Many of these persons who are now termed unemployable are casualties of an economic war which has taken a toll as definite as any military campaign, and their care is equally a national problem as the maintenance of "burnt-out" veterans of the great war.
That is something we must keep in mind in dealing with the question of unemployment and unemployment relief. When we speak about unemployables we must realize that the greater percentage would not be unemployable in times when industry was functioning normally. If a person is not in good condition, both mentally and physically, four years of enforced unemployment will make him in almost every case unemployable.

Relief and Agricultural Distress
In dealing with this matter I suggest that the government keep this in mind and try not to put these men in the same position as that in which indigent persons would be put in normal times.
During his speech yesterday, the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) referred to the fact that no leadership had been given in parliament, or for that matter outside parliament, in connection with the problems with which we are confronted today. The hon. member was criticized to-day for the statements he had made and I do not intend to add anything to that criticism. However, I should like to point out that if we are to provide leadership that will bring about any constructive action, first of all we must be agreed as to what is the cause of our difficulty. We may be lost, but if we cannot agree upon the path that is to lead us out of our difficulty, there is no hope of our getting out. There can be no effective leadership in this parliament as long as the government with their overwhelming majority will not be convinced that something must be done. As long as they believe that a policy of laissez faire will get us out of our difficulties there will be no use in trying to provide leadership. The hon. member for Kootenay East went on to refer to the cause of our present day difficulty in these words:
I need take only one illustration;-
He was referring to the change that had taken place during the last few years of our economic life.
... it is commonly known, yet nothing is done. In the last few years machinery has displaced literally tens of thousands of workers. That is a platitude; no one should be entitled to any credit for having said it, but the fact remains that neither the leaders of industry, the leaders of parliament nor the leaders of finance are paying much attention to those hordes of people thrown out of work; nor are they attempting to solve the problem of distribution or the social problem that arises therefrom. We know the situation but we are doing next to nothing to face the fact. I
I quote from page 2318 of Hansard. That point has been brought to the attention of this house, not only by the members of the group to which I belong, who have continually harped upon it in the last eight years, but by members on all sides. Economic literature everywhere is full of it. However, we act as though we were living under normal conditions. As the hon. member for Kootenay East said yesterday, never again can we hope to go back to the conditions that existed prior to 1929. It would be just as easy to go back to those times as it would be for a chick to go

back into the shell, once it is out. The hon. member said also that an economic revolution had taken place.
Referring again to the monthly letter of the Canadian Bank of Commerce, I note they point out that the improvement in employment during the last few years has not kept pace with the increase in the population. While there has been a twenty per cent increase in the population, I believe from 1928 to the end of 1937, the increase in employment was only seven per cent. If there had been no depression at all, we would still have thirteen per cent more unemployed than we had in 1928.

I shall quote from my authority, as follows:
Since 1923 the number of potential workers has increased. In addition there are those who, owing to years of enforced idleness or other causes, are no longer classed as wage earners. As compared with 1933, the rate of increase in employment has been more than double that of available labour, but we are still far from the favourable situation in 1928 (when, according to the calculations of the bureau, there were 60,000 unemployed, the post-war low record) for the labour population has increased since by about twenty per cent, while the rise in the number of employed has been less than seven per cent.

speechtext: The labour population.

speechtext:
The labour population. I think I have made that point quite clear. I am sure that the Minister of Labour, for whose intelligence I have a great respect, is well aware of the tremendous changes that have taken place in the mechanism of industry during the last twenty years. No one can be unaware of those changes who has paid any attention at all to what has been going on around us.
During the Easter holidays I paid a brief visit to the United States, to the New England states, and browsing through an old book store in Boston I came across a diary of the date

Relief and Agricultural Distress
of 1837. Boston to-day is a city of about 800,000, but there are large manufacturing and residential sections surrounding it bringing the total population up to about two million. The population of Boston in 1837, as given by this diary, was 45,000. If we want to get an idea of what has happened during the last one hundred years and a clear picture of what is wrong to-day, we should realize that the population of the United States in the last one hundred years has increased from a comparatively few million to about 130,000,000 to-day. And not only has that happened, but a whole continent has been transformed from primeval forest and virgin prairie into cities with their teeming millions, belts of steel, railroads amounting to 142,000 miles, and roads of concrete-a vast network all over the country. The same thing has been taking place on a lesser scale in the Dominion of Canada; but does anyone believe that during the next one hundred years we can build on this continent cities like New York, Chicago, Philadelphia or the other huge cities they have in the United States? We cannot, and because we cannot there is no possibility of our resuming or going through a period of economic activity such as this country has gone through in past years.

speechtext: Is imy hon. friend not aware that at the present time in the larger cities surrounding Boston there is desperate poverty and people are pauperized owing to conditions in the cotton industry?

subsubtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
I agree. We are all
pauperized except the few who own everything, and they do not know what to do with it. I saw just as much poverty, perhaps more poverty, there than I have seen here, and I also saw more wealth there. Wherever you have great wealth you have great poverty.

subsubtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Is it not possible that a country like China with its hundreds and hundreds of millions of poor people may wake up and require for the next fifty or one hundred years the things that we have in our western civilization, and so bring about the situation which my hon. friend says will not arise?

subsubtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
My hon. friend's question is this: Is it not possible that a country like China with its teeming millions of poor, lacking many things which we have in our western civilization, may one day wake up and demand a higher standard of living and industrialize their country? That is quite possible; but let me remind my hon. friend that with world machinery in the state it is in at the present time, the building up
and industrializing of China would take only a comparatively few years, and what would happen then? We would then have an industrialized China with its teeming millions competing with the rest of the world. So there is no escape in that direction. Let us not fool ourselves that we are going to better our present position by 'building up competitors to compete for the dwindling world markets which we are trying to get. That is the folly of the point of view of my hon. friend.

subsubtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: That is a good Tory speech.

subsubtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
No Tory could ever possibly think of it.
I was in the relief administrator's office a few days ago, and I saw there an illuminating chart of the trend of unemployment since 1931 or 1932; I am not quite sure of the year. I would suggest that hon. members who are interested in the problem should call on the commissioner of unemployment relief and see this chart. It is ten or twelve feet long, and the lines are so striking that one cannot fail to see them. One line shows unemployment, the drought areas included. The other shows unemployment outside the drought areas. The peak was reached in April, 1933. Then there was a slow zigzag until at the beginning of 1937 the line came down, making almost a complete diagonal; buit then, beginning this fall, the line starts to go up again. I have forgotten the exact figures; but the line came down to indicate approximately 500,000 people receiving relief, and now it has gone up again in the last six months until the figure of those receiving relief has reached the million mark, and the two lines make a complete "V." So long as that condition remains; so1 long as we are subject to these sharp fluctuations in employment, we cannot pretend that we have dealt satisfactorily or comprehensively or definitely with the question of unemployment.

Mr. J.-A. BONNIER (St. Henry) (Translation) : Mr. Speaker, I wish to say that I do not share the views of the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Howard) on the subject of housing loans. It has always been my contention that such loans are prejudicial to the interests of

Relief and Agricultural Distress
present owners of houses. In the city of Montreal, there are a great number of dwellings that have been built especially for renting purposes. We had numerous owners of three or four dwellings. Not a few of them have lost their houses and those who still hold theirs find it hard to meet their obligations, which bear interest at eight, seven or at least six per cent, while the government would loan money at only four per cent. Therefore such a scheme would create competition for the existing property owners, who have laboured hard to keep their houses and would have to continue paying interest at seven per cent, while the new ones would pay only three or four per cent.
I think there would be a more logical method of doing away with direct relief. Particularly in Montreal, a great amount of work could be undertaken in the interest of the entire country. The hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. Walsh) appeared to be opposed, earlier in the session, to the completion of the railway terminals. I think he is wrong on that point, because such terminals should be completed without delay.
I do not think there is in all Canada such a decrepit railway station as the one we have in Montreal, the metropolis of the Dominion. -In all smaller cities you will find a neat-looking station adapted to the needs of the place. Montreal is the only city to have such a terminal as Bonaventure station, built over a hundred years ago.
The hon. member for Mount Royal said the other day that the proposed completion of the terminals was an election promise. I shall tell him in reply, Mr. Speaker, that this work was undertaken many years ago, at a time when there could not possibly have been any thought of a by-election in the electoral division of St. Henry.
As to the long-projected tunnel, I think it is in 1906 that Mr. F. D. Monk mentioned the need of a tunnel at that place, and it is in 1929, if I am not mistaken, that by order in council a certain sum was made available for its construction. Therefore, it is not a new project, it is not an election promise, but a promise made as a result of reports submitted more than fifteen years ago which established the absolute necessity of such an undertaking. In Mr. Monk's time, about 15,000 persons lived beyond the canal, instead of
35,000	to-day, not including the 25,000 residents of Verdun, about one-third of the population of that city, who are obliged to cross the bridge. Is it not the government's duty

to build this tunnel which the people of the neighbourhood have so long needed? Of all the bridges crossing the Lachine canal, none is more inconvenient than the one situated in my constituency. Boats drift down the stream for about three-quarters of a mile before arriving at the bridge, the current not being swift at that point because of the locks situated 300 feet from the bridge. The ships advance very slowly to enter the locks. Quite frequently there will be another boat coming out of the locks at low speed, and people have to wait at each end of the bridge. After a fairly long wait the other day I decided to pass to the left and count the vehicles waiting to cross. There were 128 vehicles and three street cars stopped at one end of the bridge.
Does that not prove that it would be possible to undertake a great amount of necessary work in Montreal, in order to do away with the famous direct relief which was initiated by the former government, but which should never have been? Would it not be possible to give employment to those who need it? Why kill their liking for work by giving them unemployment relief? If we are to maintain the present system, it will soon be impossible to find apprentices, workers, bricklayers or carpenters to undertake necessary work in future years. To my mind, such essential projects as the completion of the Montreal terminals, the taking away of railway tracks which block the traffic and the canal in St. Henry, the building of a tunnel to enable people in that district to travel to their work with more ease, should be completed without delay in order to alleviate the burden of unemployment relief, and without creating competition for certain classes of our population.

I hesitate to participate in this debate because, after all, it seems to me a shame to find fault with what is being so honestly attempted. Yet one cannot speak on this occasion without finding a certain amount of fault, and that is a habit quite contrary to my nature. Perhaps if I put the matter clearly, it will not be so objectionable.
In the first place, in my judgment this bill is a complete disappointment; it is a failure; it offers the people of Canada a stone when they ought to have bread, and I see very little excuse for it. This country is perhaps better off, better fitted for progressive action, than any other country on the face of the earth. There is no excuse for such a lagging policy with respect to our

Relief and Agricultural Distress
economic life as we are now debating; and I maintain that our policy is lagging; it is second rate or third rate or fourth rate or worse. This may sound rather harsh, but I believe that under the circumstances it is certainly not too harsh.
One thing which worries me, which I have mentioned once or twice in this house, is that we have become completely deceived. I came into the building this morning with a gentleman who fell into step with me and who told me that he comes from the maritime provinces. Before we parted we developed a certain measure of heat between us because he maintained stoutly that there were plenty of jobs in this country if people were ready to take them. Now, whenever a man says a thing like that in my presence, after what I know and what I think any one with sense in his head ought to know, it is beyond my power to comprehend his state of mind. I challenged him to find jobs and he said, "They are here," and with a toss of his head he went on. What passed through my mind was the supercilious, the deliberately indifferent, callous attitude which the people are reported to have taken before the French revolution, and as a result of which they ignored apparently the most obvious signs that anybody ought to have been able to see. I fear there is too great a tendency towards that very thing in our public life throughout Canada, and every bit of contact I have with it makes me anxious. I beg the minister's pardon then for making an observation which might be somewhat distasteful. I was a little displeased When he stood up, with all the intelligence which I know he has, and in all apparent sincerity endeavoured to make it appear as though the Liberal party's policy had been responsible for the recovery in Canada. I am reminded of an account which I read not very long ago of the election of 1896. The background of that election, or the economic situation attendant upon it, was something like this. For a generation or two prior to 1898 there had been a great scarcity of money in the world, and because the people had the gold mentality they thought that if they did not have gold it did not make a particle of difference how many goods and services they had; they simply had to go hungry because they had no gold. In 1896 a Liberal government was elected on this side of the line, and a Republican government with exactly opposite principles was elected on the other side.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: And a great period of prosperity succeeded 1896.

subsubtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
In 1896 the Liberals are reported to have used as one of their battle-cries, perhaps not the all important one, but one of their battle-cries, "Kill the tariff and trample upon its carcass." The Republicans used just the opposite battle-cry. They put their policies into operation as far as they felt they could, I suppose, and then in 1898 there was a discovery of gold in the Klondike. As a result of that discovery and of similar discoveries in other parts of the world, there was a great influx into the world's stream of gold, consequently a great increase in the world's money and consequently a rise in prices. And, would you believe it, sir, both the Liberal administration on this side of the line and the Conservative administration on the other side of the line claimed credit for the pick-up in business.
That sort of thing I look upon as a real danger. If I have not said often enough to satisfy my hon. friends that I have no desire to be political, I hope I shall impress them by saying it once more. Whether or not the Liberal party or the Conservative party succeeds makes not the slightest difference to me; what I am concerned about is Canada. Therefore, an attempt to give a twist to improvement in world conditions; to put upon it an interpretation that is not justifiable, is, I believe, exceedingly offensive to all of us because it helps us to blind ourselves to the truth.
I am going to read a quotation from a very respectable authority.

If the hon. gentleman will give me a chance to say my say without incessant interruption, he will enjoy it better and so shall I. I am not talking social credit now; why should I be interrupted every half minute as I was the last time. On page 303 of this book I find the following words:
Needless to say, countries which do not play an active part in the rearmament race also enjoy its beneficial effects, without suffering its disadvantages in the form of a considerable increase of their public debt. From this point of view the British dominions and Latin America have been in a particularly favourable position since the beginning of the rearmament race.
Hon. members will notice what bearing that is likely to have on Canada.
It was mainly the large demand for raw materials in connection with rearmament that broke the back of the economic depression. All the reflationary efforts of President Roosevelt and other statesmen until about 1935-
It was just about that time that the Liberals came in.
-did not produce any results comparable with those brought about by the rearmament during 1935 and 1936. The frozen commodity stocks which even in 1935 consituted an important problem and a major obstacle to genuine recovery have become liquidated within a relatively short time. In some instances there is now, in fact, an excess of demand, and the restrictions imposed upon production since 1929 are being gradually abandoned.
The whole continent of South America has recovered economically and financially during 1936, far beyond the most optimistic anticipations.
Hon. members may feel entitled to credit for the pick-up in Canada; but I do not suppose anyone, even on the Liberal side would claim credit for what is happening in South America.
Even Chile, which, after the crisis of 1931 was considered to be the darkest spot on the gloomy world, shows signs of becoming prosperous and solvent. No wonder, since her two main articles of export are nitrates and copper-
At page 304 we find these words:
Could we view the situation without regard for its political, social and humane aspects, we might arrive at the conclusion that by breaking the back of the depression, rearmament was, in fact, a blessing in disguise.

We further learn from the same part of the book that even Brazil and Argentina, under influence of increased demand, have begun to relax restrictions against trade.
We are not discussing trade to-night; but in order to be realistic in facing the question of trade, there are one or two observations that, I think, should be made. There are many people who say that we ought to get together and break down trade barriers, because it is the trade barriers that are causing all the trouble. But the facts clearly indicate that the trouble is causing the trade barriers. Now the question as to what is the trouble is what we are engaged in answering to-night. Without an attempt to answer that question, talk on this subject is idle. I would call to the attention of the house the fact that this rearmament program has been financed, not with savings, but with new money. Hon. members have heard me declare that until I know they are tired of hearing it; but they must hear it again and again; for in that principle lies the only hope of salvation for this country and other countries of the British Empire. And that new money has been created by bankers. So I hope that next time the minister stands before us and introduces a bill, he will not try to claim for the Liberal administration all the credit for any improvement in conditions. No one in this parliament has been more ready to grant credit where credit is due than I; I think my speeches as reported in Hansard will bear out that statement. But if we are interested in arriving at the truth, let us refrain from statements which merely becloud the issue,
I shall not accuse the minister of the attempt, but it seemed to me there was an attempt to make our apparent recovery a little more glowing than it really is. I am just as anxious as anyone to see the doughnut, but it is well to know there is a hole in it, how big the hole is and how near we are to the edge of it. I grant that there was considerable pick-up in the business of the country; yet as the horn, member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) pointed out by reference to a monthly letter of one of the banks, there is now such a falling off that it is alarming. Let me quote briefly from the letter of the Bank of Montreal of April 22, 1938. On the second page the economic situation of the various provinces is discussed:
Quebec-While the volume of wholesale trade shows little change from that of last month it is below a year ago. Retail trade continues quiet. Collections are fair. The steel industries have benefited from recent large contracts for railway equipment and improved demand for mining machinery and agricultural implements. Many of the silk and rayon mills have

further curtailed output. Cotton factories are operating well below capacity. Furniture manufacturers have reduced operations on account of lessening demand. Lumber markets have been dull but in general stocks are not unduly burdensome. Pulpwood is in light demand, with prices weak. Newsprint mills are still operating on substantially reduced schedules.
I leave Quebec to deal with Ontario:
Ontario-Wholesale and retail trade was comparatively quiet during March and volume was below that of a year ago. With the arrival of warmer weather, however, business has shown moderate improvement. Collections are slow to fair. Knitting, textile, woollen and worsted mills as well as canners, shoe manufacturers and rubber tire companies generally, are on shorter hours with reduced working forces, although hosiery mills and rubber footwear factories remain busy. A number of steel companies report increased activity as the result of large orders for railway, mining and transportation equipment as well as war materials, and aircraft companies are very busy. Mining activity continues at record levels.
These last statements tend to show that it is rearmament which is causing the apparent prosperity. On the third page the maritime provinces are dealt with:
Maritime provinces-Wholesale and retail volume is running somewhat below last year's levels. Collections are fair. Raw fur sales have been disappointing and prices show a sharp recession. Dried fish markets are quiet. Canned lobster is moving slowly, with heavy stocks on hand. The market for long lumber is weak and prices have declined. I
I think that is sufficient; I shall not read any more. The situation in Canada is not nearly as bright as the minister seemingly has forced himself to think it is. In this house we should face conditions as they are. I do not believe the Liberal government are alone responsible for this situation. They have gone out and got more markets; I grant that. But without a change of system, the policy of neither the Liberal nor the Conservative party can cure the difficulties of this country. I am confident that this will become more and more apparent as the days go by. I only hope it will become apparent to a sufficiently large number of people before it is too late to do something. But the opportunity is passing. Conditions in many places in this country are positively terrible. That gentleman who talked with me this morning and so glibly assured me that there are plenty of jobs, came from an area not far from where this letter was written. This letter came to me personally, with no idea that it would ever be read in parliament. It comes right from the hearts of men who are in the midst of this terrible misery in a time when we are soothing ourselves into the idea that conditions are
reasonably good. It comes from Nova Scotia.

speechtext:
Very good. I would much rather have that happen, now that hon. members have heard it, because, after all, I am more concerned with having hon. members in the house know about existing conditions than I am that the letter appear in Hansard. I am not going to expose a man who writes a letter like that to me.
All right; having said this much, I wish to pass on to another consideration. I have heard a good deal since I came to the house about those fine old virtues of hard work and thrift, and stern, stubborn self-help, faith in the future, and all those things.
On those principles our country was builded. There are a number of people who so far deceive themselves as to think that we social crediters do not believe that. No bigger piece of delusion can be conceived by man. We cannot build a state or a strong community without hard work, thrift, stern and stubborn self-help, faith in the future, patriotism, unity and democracy. I maintain that the greatest condemnation of the government in power to-day is that it is rendering those very virtues utterly impossible for a large part of the population of Canada. There is no successful contravention of what I say. We have hundreds of thousands of people throughout Canada who cannot get work at all, much less hard work, of profitable value. They will do anything to get work.

The one thing, sir, we cannot afford to lose in this country is the productive value of the human being. We are ignoring it, neglecting it, spurning it and rendering it utterly futile. We have been doing that for nine years. Surely, if this has not proved the absolute ineptitude of the present system, I do not know how much proof hon. members need. How many generations of failure must we have before we become convinced the present system cannot work any more?
Thrift! How can men save when they cannot get enough to keep body and soul together? Hon. members know that hundreds of thousands of people in Canada find it impossible to have any kind of meagre savings, from the contemptible incomes which they derive. Where, then, is the training for thrift? How is it possible? We must change this system, or no more shall we have genuine thrift in Canada.
The incomes sufficiently large to enable people to save to any great extent are being drawn by only a very small proportion of our population, and that proportion is steadily decreasing.
Stem, stubborn self-help! Men have thrown themselves against walls of reality until their bodies and spirits are bruised and broken, in their attempt to get along without assistance. Finally, they fall back in utter helplessness. How can people have faith in the future? From the very letter, a portion of which I have already read, I could read a statement indicating that these people are beginning to wonder what it was they fought for. We aire building up a fine public attitude, a splendid morale, to go through another test, such as the last war! We are forcing the very kind of youth who, twenty years ago, sprang together to defend the country, into sudh disgraceful and degrading conditions, degrading to both body and spirit, that they have no heart whatsoever to fight. They say, "What have we to lose?"
I say if we are interested in the welfare of Canada-and I am sure every hon. member is-we simply must make a change, so as to give these people, these youth who are growing up, confidence that Canada is a land to love, and not a land to oppress them. We are oppressing them, disgracefully.
We hear a great deal about unity. We hear a great deal about the need for patriotism and democratic principles. When I hear that, I am reminded of a person who, suffering from rheumatism, applies some salve and hot flannels, and draws near the stove. He does anything and everything but try to remove the cause. The measure before us

Relief and Agricultural Distress
to-night is nothing but a palliative. There is no attempt whatsoever to find the cause of the difficulty, much less to remove it.
Some people would say: "What would you do about it?" In the first place, let us be sure that we must do something more than we are doing now. Just as soon as hon. members are agreed that what we are now doing is not sufficient, just that soon will we be ready and humble enough to go to the trouble of using some other methods. I shall read from the words of a man for whom I believe every hon. member has at least a measure of respect, namely Mr. Anthony Eden. If hon. members will permit me, I shall take the liberty of making comments as I read, because I believe this article contains a grave message for us in Canada, as it does for Great Britain and for all democratic countries. It has a direct bearing on what I was saying a few moments ago about unity and democracy. The Ottawa Citizen of Wednesday, April 27, quotes Mr. Eden as saying:
It would be foolish, perhaps fatal to the very survival of democracy, to ignore the stupendous achievements realized under other forms of government. A truly immense effort has been made in the last few years by autocratic states for the fulfilment of the purposes they have set before them.
Their methods cannot be ours, but we should not fail to note the passionate fervour with which they are being realized.
Contrast the passionate fervour which they are demonstrating according to Anthony Eden with the lethargy which is manifested in this country, with the disposition to let things ride and wait for something to turn up! I continue with the quotation:
If we are to uphold our idea, our conception of life, both national and international, if we are to see them prevail, then a comparable effort must be made by us and an equal spirit be roused. This is a time when every endeavour should be made to promote national unity, for it is only as a united nation that we can give of our best.
Party warfare for its own sake should have no place in the scheme of things to-day. A united effort for the spiritual and material rearmament of the nation is the need of the hour.
It would be hard to find words that are more appropriate to conditions as they exist at this moment. I maintain that we are not taking such measures as will build up the spiritual and material resources of this country. We all hope it may not be so, but we all fear that we are approaching a most dreadful time of testing when practically every part of our being is unprepared. People will say, "What will you do about it?" First of all, I say that we are going to do something.
Then it will be asked, "What will that something be?" I have been much interested in the proposals which have been made. I was particularly interested in the speech of the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Howard), and I think it did him great credit. I have been interested in the proposals of hon. members who have suggested that we should conduct irrigation work; that we should have extensive reforestation and road construction. These suggestions are all perfectly sound. The hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Marsh) made a most entertaining and interesting speech yesterday, as did the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens).
But in each instance I am sure hon. members felt that we have only so much money; that all we can get is what we can tax from the people or borrow. It would not be wise to borrow any more. We want to balance the budget if it lies within our power, and we should begin to pay off our debts. We are taxing our people to the absolute limit. Well, then, they would say, "Hon. member, which one of the things upon which we are now spending money would you have us curtail? If we cannot curtail in any respect; if we cannot get money in any other way, then how in the world do you think we can finance these projects?" That is what it amounts to as surely as we are here in this building. Where are you going to get the money? I am not going to make any extended comments to-night. I am not going to talk about social credit in any detail as some hon. member would rise probably to a point of order and oppose my remarks. Without any reflection upon those who preside, I must say it seems strange that those who are called to order are the ones who try to offer suggestions which would really improve matters.
I want to remind hon. members that the money with which the war preparations are being financed is credit; it is not savings. Let us get that thoroughly into our thinking. Where does that credit come from? Undoubtedly the bankers all over the world are producing it. Is the Canadian banking system producing any part of it? If it is, then can we not arrange things so that our bankers will be able to produce the credit which we need to improve conditions in our country? The minute we begin to think along that line, we shall begin to see a way out of the difficulty in which we find ourselves. I say earnestly and frankly that if the Dominion of Canada would begin an earnest study of the principles of social credit, a way could be found out of our difficulties.

I think I can safely venture to say that if wisdom and industry were used in the application of these principles, the Minister of Labour would never again be humiliated by having to bring down, a bill such as this. There would be no further need for a bill to relieve unemployment in this country. If anything more is needed, I am willing to say it. I have such confidence in the principles of social credit that I feel sure that would be the result. Absurd? Of course it sounds absurd, but everything new sounds absurd.

speechtext:
Just a word to explain
why I said that the report of the employment commission was rotten. It is because the figures contained in the twenty-ninth tabulation of statistics at the end of the report do not indicate the previous occupations of the unemployed. They refer to the last time the unemployed had any occupation; they give some information about the ages of the unemployed, their capacity or incapacity to work; but they do not tell what those unemployed did before they became unemployed, or where they live. For those reasons the statistics published in the report are absolutely useless, although quite a lot of work may have been involved in compiling them. Besides that, what I find foolish is the calculation of the percentage to one-tenth. It was absolutely absurd.
I strongly objected to the appointment of Mr. Purvis as the chairman. My contention at the time was that no one knew better the problem of unemployment than any member of this house who has occasion to meet unemployed persons either during the session or during the recess and to be in contact with

Relief and Agricultural Distress
them. Mr. Purvis has no occasion to meet any unemployed. He may shake hands at times with the men who are working in the numerous institutions of which he is a director, but on the other hand he never meets any unemployed. Therefore he knows nothing about their real lives and their troubles and miseries.
There was one thing that struck me. When the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe asked the Minister of Labour two years ago what salary was to be paid to Mr. Purvis, the minister gave an evasive answer; he did not at the time answer yes or no. The member for Temiscouata repeated his offer to do the work of classification for nothing, providing that he could take a few civil servants at his own choice to assist him in that compilation. Afterwards Mr. Purvis was put to shame and said that he was not charging anything; in fact, he received, I admit, nothing apparently in gold or in paper money or in social credit money. But, on the other hand, he did something which was most unethical and for which he should be deported at once as undesirable. There are two reports, one on unemployment and one on employment. As to the large report on employment, which contains data of January, 1937, about those engaged in industry, it should not be forgotten that Mr. Purvis, the chairman of the national employment commission, is also chairman and managing director of Canadian Industries Limited, president of the Dunlop Tire and Rubber Company Limited, and of numerous other institutions. Therefore Mr. Purvis as head of the commission secured confidential information about all industries, some twenty-seven or twenty-nine of them. That report is more fully detailed than the report on unemployment, and especially on the chemical industry, the industry of chemical products, and on the industry of rubber products, in which he is interested.

Also as president and chairman of Canadian Industries Limited he was highly interested to know what was going on in the chemical industry. He knew it all. Perhaps that is the reason why he was exhausted after his report was tabled. I find it, sir, most unethical for a man, who stated he was asking nothing to do that work, to take advantage of his position as chairman of a public body to secure private information for which other industrialists would be ready to pay half a million or a million dollars That is one point.

For public purposes. But he took personal advantage of it; and private replies, mentioning the names were sent to the commission by the industries concerned. The figures that he gave did not disclose the information that he had, because he gave them for the Dominion of Canada and for the province at large, not naming a single industry, when personally he had that information. Tom Moore said nothing on that. I objected strongly also to the appointment of Tom Moore, whom I did not name in 1936, for the reason that he has done nothing in his life and cannot teach others how to work. Moreover, the conclusions of the report are silly. One of them is to amplify the employment offices, to give a job to Tom Moore. If he was in distress he could secure direct relief. And the social insurance, which he has advocated as chairman of the trades and labour congress every time he appeared before the government, in the eyes of the national employment commission seems to be a plan to secure a job for Tom Moore-quite an expensive undertaking.
Sir, I will say nothing more for the moment on this matter than this. Why did the government have to appoint the national employment commission instead of naming a parliamentary committee of the House of Commons to study the matter of unemployment? Was it not because in the very Department of Labour the minister did not have the assistance that he was supposed to have from all his officials? I have nothing to say about the unemployment relief branch; I have the highest respect for three gentlemen who occupy prominent positions in that branch, Mr. Hereford, Mr. Houston and Mr. Carter, and some others who are doing good work in minor positions. The former deputy minister of labour was at one time a railway man, a man with a good education and a good knowledge of railway problems, and in the discharge of his duties he rendered good service to the state. Imagine that man being replaced by a man who was a former private secretary of the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, who had several years' experience as private secretary to ministers, and whose only experience with regard to the unemployed was six years in the remission branch of the Department of Justice dealing with convicts. It seems to me a shame that Mr. Ward was forced to resign to give place to that man, a man not qualified. The minister may deny that; but I am sure that if he had had, as deputy minister of labour, Mr. Ward, who was a very capable man, whom I knew

personally, and who helped me in some work I did on behalf of the unemployed, we would have had no employment commission. That is all I have to say for the moment.

subsubtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: I have expressed at various times my admiration for the independence of the hon. member for Temiseouata, but at this time I wish to take strong exception to some of the observations he has just made. I will say this very definitely, that from my contact with the members of the national employment commission, each and every one of them accepted the responsibilities of that commission with a keen sense of public obligation. My hon. friend has referred particularly to Mr. Purvis, who was chairman of the commission. Mr. Purvis accepted the chairmanship of the commission at the request of the government. Naturally the government was responsible for his selection, and so far as I have had association with Mr. Purvis as chairman of the commission I am absolutely convinced that he gave honestly and wholeheartedly his best effort to the task in hand. My hon. friend is entitled to take exception to any or all of the recommendations of the commission; but I do not think there should be any imputation cast upon the motives either of the chairman of that commission or of other members of it, and I think that applies equally to the members of the public service of Canada. I wish to make that statement immediately so that there shall be no misunderstanding of my position.

subsubtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: I did not impute any motives; I stated facts.

subsubtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: I have no brief whatever for Mr. Purvis. I have not the pleasure of knowing him; but if I have his history, he is a self-made man who employs people; and what astounds me so much is that people who, as far as I know, never employed any one at all, 'have the impudence to criticize a man of that type.

subsubtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
I have no desire to follow along the lines pursued by the hon. member for Temiseouata. I have nothing against any of the gentlemen mentioned, and I think it is sometimes unfortunate that aspersions should foe cast upon people who are not here to defend themselves. I have never met Mr. Purvis in my life and I would not know him if I did meet him, but I believe he is an honourable man and that he acted in an honourable capacity. I might disagree with the conclusions he arrived at and with the recommendations submitted to the government, but that would not prevent me from

Relief and Agricultural Distress
at least giving him credit for being an honourable .person. And so far as Tom Moore is concerned, I think the remarks that were made are entirely undeserved. Mr. Moore used to work as hard as any member of this house. He was by trade a carpenter until he was made a paid official of the trades and labour congress, and I cannot understand what the hon. member for Temiscouata has against him in his capacity as a member of the national employment commission.
However, I want to get down to something definite in connection with the matter before us. I do not wish to discuss personalities in a matter of such far-reaching importance as unemployment relief. I want to deal with one aspect of the question of relief which has come to my attention in the past few weeks. It is the attempt which is being made in Winnipeg, and probably in other parts of Canada, to reduce the standard of relief being given to persons who are unfortunately the recipients of public assistance. Not only is an effort being made to reduce the standard of relief given, probably in order to save costs to the national and local exchequers, but there are also new regulations being put into force, which in my opinion will have an extremely serious effect upon the general standard of living of the persons involved. In Winnipeg, those who determine the kind of relief are putting into effect certain regulations which provide that when a person is working he will be allowed to spend only so much of his salary per week or per month, and the balance is to be put away for a time when he may find himself in the ranks of the unemployed. The amount allowed to be spent in Winnipeg is not much more than the amount they receive when on relief. At the present time people on relief have exhausted practically everything that they have, and they will not be allowed to replenish anything; they will be compelled to live on a basis not much better than that which they experienced when they were recipients of public relief. It means that these people are going to be driven to a very low standard of living, so that they drag down the higher standards that others may have attained as a result of many years of endeavour. I cannot too strongly condemn regulations of that kind. I want to know if that is the policy of the government or whether they acquiesce in a policy of that kind being adopted by public authorities.

subsubtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
My answer to my hon. friend is that the dominion government has not in any way brought pressure to bear upon
provincial governments with respect to any change in relief scales. We have from time to time altered our grants in aid to provincial governments; in doing so, we have been influenced by improvement in the unemployment situation in those provinces and to some extent by improvement in the financial position of certain provinces. Those have been the two factors which have always governed grants in aid by the dominion to the provinces. But there has been no pressure ol any kind in respect of relief scales. That is something which, as my hon. friend is no doubt aware, is dealt with entirely by provincial governments in conjunction with the municipalities. There is no uniform relief scale throughout the dominion; there is not in the municipalities in a province; it varies not only between provinces but as between municipalities in the same province.

subsubtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Does not a representative of the Department of Labour confer with the authorities in the different provinces and in that way control in some measure the scale of relief being given?

subsubtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: No. The only possible connection that might exist between the dominion government and relief scales is a clause in the agreements covering the last quarter of the past fiscal year which stated that the relief allowances should not compete, so to speak, with the prevailing wage in a municipality. I have mentioned that before in this house. That is the only clause of the agreement that I can recall at the moment which would have any effect upon relief scales as applied in any particular municipality.

subsubtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Some time ago I asked the minister some questions in reference to the highest relief scale paid anywhere in Canada and the relief scale which was competing with wage scales in any part of Canada. Could I have an answer now?

subsubtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: I remember the question, and I think my friend will recall that I stated that I doubted the wisdom of giving the relief scales prevailing in each city. It is not a matter which is within the control of the dominion government; it is determined wholly by the municipality in question. As for the other information asked by my hon. friend, I shall be glad to take note of it and see that it is made available.

subsubtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
I did not want the minister to give me the locality; I just wanted the highest relief scale.

subsubtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: I can secure that information, and shall do so. I thought the hon. member wished me to state what particular locality had this high relief scale.

subsubtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: The minister says that the department has requested the provincial authorities that relief scales shall not compete with prevailing rates of wages. I think in that they are taking a dangerous step. I could understand that, assuming relief scales were extremely high, the departmental officials might think that people would not be anxious to accept work at prevailing rates. They might claim that. I do not know of any relief scale in Canada that competes with what I would call fair rates of pay. The minister and other members of the committee will understand that there is a difference between what might be called prevailing rates and fair rates of pay. The prevailing rate in some area might be fifteen cents an hour; I know of instances of men working a whole week and at the end of the week getting the magnificent sum of $9 to maintain themselves and their family. I do not think there is any hon. member who would blame a man if he would not work for fifteen cents an hour. But if that happened to be the prevailing rate of pay, it might occur that a person having no alternative but relief would be compelled to accept it or have the relief allowance reduced accordingly. The department cannot avoid responsibility for conditions of that kind. A few months ago there was brought to my attention a place in Canada where that low rate of wages was being paid. In the case of Winnipeg I know what the relief rate is; I think I referred to it just prior to the recess. For a married couple, if my memory is correct, it was about $20 a month, or even less than that. I know it was extremely low. I am afraid that the tendency will be to reduce the scale still further, lowering the standard of living and wages as well. I want to prevent that. I do not want to see people on relief in Canada; I am one of those who for years have deplored the fact that the government has been compelled to give relief to people out of work. I would far rather see the government undertake a vast scheme of public works across this country to provide work for those in need, with a scale of pay in conformity, not with prevailing rates, but with either union rates or fair wages as determined by provincial regulation.

subsubtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: But my hon. friend on one occasion condemned that solution of the problem. I take it he has not changed his mind on that.

subsubtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
As a final solution, I still say no. But I think we agree that although a scheme of public works is not a final solution, it at least alleviates the condition. It would be far better for the people who are to-day receiving relief to be performing some useful work.
